The PRIME MINISTER (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier) moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 47) to amend the Act to restrict the importation and employment of aliens. He said : The leading feature of the first amendment which is proposed by this Bill concerns the third section of the present Act, which provides for a penalty for a violation of this Act of $l,O0J, no more and no less. The object of the amendment is to make the penalty not more than $1,001) and not less than $50, giving to the judge discretion to apply the penalty according to the offence. Then, it is stated in the Act that tlie penalty is to be recovered only by the consent of the Attorney General. We propose to modify that section, and to provide that the penalty shall be recovered with the consent, either of the Attorney General of the province, or of the judge of any court in which the penalty is sued for.
The second amendment concerns section 5 of the Act. I have not the Act before me, but section 5 provides that a settler, that is to say, an intending settler, may bring with him a relative or a personal friend. It has been found in practice that this word ' personal friend ' is too elastic for practical purposes, and that it may be made an occasion for evading the law ; therefore, we propose to strike out the words * personal friend.'
Section (i of the said Act provides that if there has beeu a violation of the Act, the party who has been introduced into tlie country illegally shall be sent back at the expense of the person previously coutraet-ing for the services. It is proposed to strike out these words, and to substitute | in lieu thereof :
At the expense of the person, partnership, company or corporation violating any of the provisions of section 1 of this Act.
Then, it is proposed to repeal section 8 of the Act altogether, and to substitute the following section therefor :
That it shall be deemed a violation of this ' Act for any person, partnership, company or corporation to assist or encourage the importation or immigration of any alien or foreigner who resides in, or is a citizen of any foreign country to which this Act shall apply, by promise of employment through advertisements, printed or published in such foreign country, and any such alien or foreigner, coming to this country in consequence of such an advertisement, shall be treated as coming under a contract as contemplated by this Act, and the penalties by this Act imposed shall be applicable in such case. Nothing in this Act contained shall be held to affect or control the government of Canada or of any provision of the Territories in respect of promoting immigration.
This last amendment has been inserted at the suggestion of the labour organizations, who have strongly pressed for its adoption.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

House resumed adjourned debate on the proposed motion of Mr. Bennett :
That, in the opinion of this House, the time has arrived when a fixed and definite line of action should be undertaken on the question of the transportation of the grain and other com-
modifies of the North-west Territories, Manitoba and the western states, with a view to centreing the same to the greatest possible extent in Canadian channels.

Mr. Speaker, this motion was before the House yesterday, and the debate was cut short at six o'clock. I had intended saying something then, but was prevented by that fact. I just wish to say a little more in regard to the transportation problem and something in regard to the features of it that were brought up in the House yesterday. I would like to take a strictly non-partisan position in regard to this transportation problem, but when I remember how the Minister of Railways and Canals (Hon. Mr. Blair) treated me last night, and has treated me on several occasions, I do not think I would be discharging my duty unless I pointed out some of the mistakes that he has made in the past in connection with this question. The other day, the recognized organ of bon. gentlemen opposite, the Globe, in Toronto, was discussing the railway question as it affected the people of Manitoba, and as it affects them to-day in relation to a certain proposition that is now before them in connection with the Canadian Northern Railway. The Globe, said that there is an element of resentment in the attitude of the people and their representatives in the matter. What gave rise to this element of resentment in the minds of the people of Manitoba ? It is because this government failed in 1898 to do what they should have done for the protection of the people in connection with certain transportation problems then before the parliament of Canada. In 1898, when we had this matter up in the House, I directed the attention of both sides of the House to the fact that a great railway proposition and a new proposition was being brought to their attention. I quoted from the Globe newspaper of that day outlining the scheme of Mann and Mackenzie, having in view the establishment of a new transportation route, and I said that this is the opportunity when so much money is being expended to protect the people of Manitoba, and to protect the whole people of Canada. I will quote from the Globe newspaper a statement of what was done in 1898 in this House, in the legislature in Toronto, and in the legislature in Manitoba, in three legislatures that were controlled absolutely by the Liberal party. The Ontario and Rainy River Railway has 286 miles in the province of Ontario, and that province gave it $1,110,000 without a single condition being imposed. The Dominion government gave $960,000 in connection with the same railway without conditions, and the province of Manitoba guaranteed bonds to the extent of $5,800,000 on the portion of the road both within the province and without it. On the whole there was

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
granted to that road $27,000 a mile of public money for 290 miles in Ontario ; $8,000 a mile guaranteed by Manitoba for the Minnesota section and the section in Manitoba ; and the Dominion government in 1898 gave 6,400 acres a mile. The Manitoba government guaranteed $10,000 a mile bonds which, with the land grants, made a donation of $20,000 a mile to that concern. In 1898 three Liberal legislatures in this country : the legislature of Ontario, the legislature of Manitoba, and this parliament controlled by the Liberal party, gave the equivalent of $20,000 a mile for this road. I called the attention of parliament and the Minister of Railways to these facts when the measure was going through here, and I said : Now is the time to protect the people of Manitoba. But the minister replied : You are wandering far afield ; you are trying to pose before the country, and he made all kinds of charges of that kind against me when my only desire was to get him to protect the interests of the people. What was the defence that the hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Blair) set up then '! He said : This is not a great continental project ; it is only a little railway and does not involve any great interest. That statement of the minister (Hon. Mr. Blair) is on record, and when 1 divided the House, the right hon. the First Minister rushed the measure through and he neglected to seize the opportunity which would have protected the people of Manitoba to-day. The people of Manitoba are now seeking to right the wrong that was perpetrated upon them by three legislatures controlled by the Liberal party. The province of Ontario is to blame for not taking some sort of satisfactory guarantee from the Rainy River road ; the minister (Hon. Mr. Blair) is to blame in the same way, and the Greenway government is most of all to blame. If what I proposed had been done, namely, to unite and make that road a national road, there would be no grievance in Manitoba to-day, but on the contrary, the Rainy River Railway would have been a link in the new national system. It would in a short time have been connected with the Crow's Nest Pass Railway and with the Intercolonial system, and for the money that Canada has expended on these railways we would have practically had a national system across the continent without costing us an additional cent. The Minister of Railways on that occasion failed to protect the interests of the country ; he failed to protect the interests of Manitoba, and the same charge applies to the Liberal governments of Ontario and Manitoba.
I want to pass, Mr. Speaker, from that partial view of the case. I am sorry to have to say of hon. gentlemen opposite that they failed in their duty. Now. with what the hon. gentleman from Simcoe (Mr. Bennett) has said in regard to transportation of Lake Superior, I agree to some extent, but I 1 do not agree with all he said, for if his argu-

ment means anything it means that the Grand Trunk Railway system from Midland to Montreal isi the system Rest adapted to solve the transportation problem, and that after we are finished with the canals we should do nothing more. I do not agree with the hon. gentleman (Mr. Bennett) in that respect. On the contrary, I agree with hon. gentlemen opposite. I say that there is or will be enough traffic for every system of transportation which we have got, and the thing for us to do is to find that system will give us the best and most immediate results. The Grand Trunk Railway has a good harbour at Midland and a good system to Montreal, but just when it reaches Montreal it does the worst thing possible for Canada, because it deflects that traffic to Portland. That should not be, nor should the Grand Trunk Railway be allowed to continue that practice. The best way to stop that and to afford a remedy is to do just what the hon. member (Mr. Bennett) said we should not do. I believe we should nationalize the Booth lines and nationalize the Ross line, and from all I can gather to-day Quebec is the natural port for a great deal of that trade. At very small cost Quebec can be made a splendid shipping port, and can be developed and put in running order this year, and extended every year in the future. I believe that there is something in winter navigation, but I do not intend to enter upon that subject to-day. Be that as it may. Quebec is the most available port we have in Canada for the greatest length of time during the year, and it can be equipped with the least expense. I believe that the Canada Atlantic Railway and the Great Northern Railway would make a first-class extension of the 'Intercolonial Railway. I do not believe that our national line, the Intercolonial Railway, should end at Montreal. I believe in its extension to the great lakes where the traffic originates and where it will find a feeder. If these ports are to be built up ; if the 200 million bushels of grain -which I believe will be 400 millions before a great while-which comes to the great lakes and which will come to Midland and to Parry Sound are to toe handled in Canada, I want to see the Grand Trunk Railway get a share of it and I want to see the Canadian national railway getting its share of it and taking it to Quebec in the summer time and to St. John, Halifax or Sydney in the winter time, or if need be. all the year around. I am applying my system of nationalizing the railways as a solution of the problem submitted to us yesterday by the hon. member (Mr. Bennett). I believe that the people of Canada are in favour of nationalizing the Booth system and the Ross system and making them part of the Intercolonial Railway. I believe that if the government had in 1898 secured a proper control over the Rainy River road, Canada would have a national system of railways in a short while right into the city of Winnipeg, and in that way we would have been able to discipline all the other railways in this country. My hon. friend from Simcoe iMr. Bennett) said that we had spent enough money on the canals and that we should now iet the railways have a show. I do not agree with him there. My opinion is that for twenty years the railways have done their best to prevent the deepening and enlarging of our canals, and now that our canal system is coming into vogue I would like to see it largely improved and extended.
We in Toronto, also believe that probably one great solution of the transportation problem is to make a national road somewhere between the Georgian Bay and Toronto, by which we could use the canal and river system from that city down to the sea.
That is the idea.

That may be the cheapest and best way out of it ; that may be the complement of what the government is today doing in the harbour of Collingwood. They are making great improvements there, and we would like to know if they are making them with the idea that they will have a railway between Toronto and Collingwood, or Toronto and Midland or wherever the port may be. The port may be Penetanguisliene. But that is a proposition which must be in the government's mind, and it may be one that will go a great way in solving the transportation problem. The only satisfactory solution of the transportation problem of this country, however, is by the parliament and government taking over the railways, and making them a complement of our canal system. When you control the railways and the canals, you can use the one or the other or the two in combination; they will work in harmony in the best interests of the country.
I wish briefly to enumerate some of the positive advantages of the nationalization of railways. It will secure the absolute control of our own lines, and absolute equality of treatment to all, rich and poor, individual and corporation. Government ownership will restore the land grants to the people, and some of the money the people put into these roads. Government ownership will make the canals and our water navigation, and all the improvements thereof, and the railway system of the country, complementary one of the other. Government ownership will necessitate the ocean terminals of our railways being at Canadian ports and in that way make our railways patriotic. The only way you can make Canadian roads patriotic is by compelling them to have their terminals at Canadian ports. Government ownership will build up a British Canadian ocean service on the Atlantic and the Pacific. Tt will secure the fullest use of all trains for a greatly im-

proved postal service. It will secure the control and extension of tlie parcel express business, and will allow of the railway telegraph service being consolidated with a national telegraph system; and all this will be secured at a much less cost than now for administration, and at a much less cost to the people who use the service. Government ownership means that a national policy with regard to railways can be made complementary to the national fiscal policy, and one will greatly aid and reinforce the other. Government ownership means lower freight rates for the producers, whether farmers, miners, lumbermen, stockmen, or fishermen. Government ownership means cheaper passenger rates, with a greatly improved passenger service. Government ownership means the opening up of new country with the money now sunk in unnecessary roads in older sections. Government ownership means that the entire energy of the management of such a national system will be devoted to the service of the people, and to solving the problem how best to handle the traffic of the country at the lowest cost to the producer or consumer, instead of wasting the best part of that energy, as is done to-day, in fighting rival roads at the expense of people along the lines or the country at large.
What are the things which the nationalization of railways will prevent or render unnecessary ? It will prevent the creation of a railway commission. If we can avoid the creation of an expensive railway commission, it will be a great point in favour of tlie nationalization of railways. Government ownership will prevent the everlasting war between such a commission and the railways which is sure to occur after the commission is created. Government ownership will prevent the unpatriotic conduct of private railways like the Grand Trunk going to Portland, and the Canadian Pacilic Hailway going to Boston. Government ownership will wipe out the frightful corruption in politics by the great corporations. Government ownership will do away with the extravagant and unnecessary extension of the present national system of railways. Government ownership will do away with the duplication of existing roads by unnecessary lines. Government ownership will avoid the expensive and extravagant system of competition for business, involving many unnecessary officials, offices, advertising, solicitors, commissions, &c. Government ownership will prevent foreign ownership and control, and the consequent unpatriotic policy that might emanate therefrom. Government ownership will prevent the hostile attitude that existing roads show to new roads coming into and getting into cities, and will put an end to all unnecessary and expensive entrances into cities and ports. Do you know what happens in a city like Toronto or Montreal when a new road wants to come in ? It involves the Mr. MACLEAN.
expenditure of millions of money, a great fight, and the waste of a tremendous amount of energy. With government ownership there will be a national entry into each city, and none of the fighting and expense now indulged in by competing roads. That alone will be an enormous saving. The more you look at this railway question in all its aspects, the more evident it becomes that the only way to avoid the troubles ahead is through government ownership. The more we do to build up rival roads, the more we complicate the problem. When you stop giving to railways, subsidies of money and lands, and gradually get control of them, you will be in a position to give the people transportation at the lowest cost.
.lust one other feature of this transportation problem I want to refer to, that is, the Atlantic service. This country has made no progress in getting an Atlantic service since this government came into power. We are rather worse off than we were before. We find our Canadian ports becoming deserted. My idea is that the government should run an Atlantic service in connection witli the Intercolonial Railway. I believe that the coming Atlantic port is Sydney. The government could make the experiment with two moderate-sized steamships, which would give a service once a week; and if it were found to pay, it would do more to advertise this country, and build up the Intercolonial and the Canadian national system of railways than anything else. The traffic would have to pass over the national railway of Canada. Not only the people of New York and Boston would use the service, but all the west would use it; and I believe that before ten years were over, we would have a fast Atlantic service running from an Intercolonial terminal, which would send a steamer across the ocean every day in the year. I believe that a fast Atlantic service is coming, and as a Canadian I would like to see it quick. The way to secure it is to hold the national system of railways which we have to-day, and gradually extend that system, and not to be afraid to go ahead and take over the other systems, which can be done at a very small expense.
As I have said before, the people of Canada to-day, are paying all the cost of these railways. It is not the companies or the shareholders who are paying for them; it is the traffic, and the greater burden you put upon the traffic by establishing unnecessary lines, the harder it is for the people to bear. There is no getting rid of the difficulties of the situation other than by coming to a straight national system of railways. -
I hope that the government will yet see its way to come out in favour of the nationalization of railways, and extend the national system to the upper lakes. We have only got a portion of the way. While I agree with a great deal that my bon. friend from Sim-

coe (Mr. Bennett) has said in criticism of the government, I do not agree in his policy of malting the Grand Trunk Railway the line over which this traffic will pass, but would prefer a line owned and controlled by the people, and which would be an extension of the Intercolonial Railway. I trust that hon. gentlemen opposite will not charge me with posing before this House, because the very policy I am advocating to-day I drew attention to three sessions ago in this House ; but I do make this charge to-day, and am sorry to have to make it-that if the government had maintained control of those roads, and the money they gave the Rainy River Railway in 1898. there would not be the trouble in Manitoba which exists there to-day. I believe, however, that the Manitobans are a self-relying people, and that they will work out a solution which will not impose any great burden on them in this connection. They are making a step in the direction of government ownership, and the province of Ontario proposes hereafter to maintain some kind of control of the railways, so that we can fairly say that government ownership is in the air ; and those politicians who first tried to impress that policy on the public and have it carried out. will be those whom the people will recognize as having had the courage of their convictions, and as having-advocated a policy which cannot fail to be beneficial in the public interest.

speakeroldname: Mr. DEPUTY SPEAKER (Mr. Peter Macdonald, East Huron).
speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
1 rise to express my views upon the transportation question irrespective of any route. The transportation question, in my opinion, is one of the most important engaging public attention. I do not regard it as a party question at all. Nor is it a local question, for we are all desirous of establishing- the very best system of conveying from one part of the country to the other the products of the energies of the Canadian people. It is not to be supposed for one moment, that any one route will carry all the products of the country. Some will go by the waterways, and some partially by waterways and partially by railways ; but it is undoubted that the most effective way of controlling railway rates is to put our waterways in the very best condition. It has been the experience everywhere that a waterway has a very-strong controlling influence upon railway-rates owing to the cheapness with which a waterway can carry the freight and traffic of the country, and the time has come when we must devise the best means of meeting the extraordinary expansion of trade we are now experiencing. Our trade is happily increasing by leaps and bounds. It would probably surprise many' who have not given attention to the figures, that in 1888, 9.000 vessels passed through the Sault Ste. Marie canal, south and w-est, the average tonnage of which was 600 tons, and the
amount of tonnage carried through was 5,495,000, and the value $79,000,000. That will give an idea of the extraordinary-trade which passed through the Sault canal in 1888. Twelve years have elapsed, and I find, on looking over the figures, that instead of 9,000 vessels having passed through last year, 20,000 vessels passed through, with an average tonnage of 1,000 tons ; and these y-essels carried, not five and a half million tons, but twenty-five million tons. And instead of the value being $79,000,000, the freight carried amounted to $218,000,000 in value. That shows the expansion of trade in Lake Superior during the past twelve years, and impresses upon us the importance of providing increased facilities for that trade, so as to prevent its being handled by a foreign country. Our government have been doing what they could to improve the greatest waterway in the world. Canada's waterway extends from the Atlantic Into the very heart of the continent, a distance of no less than 2,700 miles, but nature, in giving us that unrivalled waterway, left some obstacles which we are in duty bound to remove as far as possible. A portion of that waterway belongs to us, and a portion is common to us and the United States. We have spent no less than $75,000,000 to $80,000,000 in constructing canals, w-hich, I think, was a wise policy. But we must remember that there are other things to be done. We have canals now 14 feet deep, which will accommodate vessels carrying from 60,000 to 100,000 bushels of wheat, but we require also deep harbours and better terminals. We sometimes lament that we are not getting more trade, but the reason is because we cannot handle satisfactorily the trade we are now receiving. The large vessels that come down laden with wheat pass in sight of Port Colborne and sail into the port of Buffalo, and one of the most important things Canada has to do is to make that Port Colborne sufficiently- deep to enable large vessels to come in and send the wheat in our direction. There is another thing required, and that is a guard pier ; and I am glad that the parliament of Canada voted money last year for the purpose of providing it. Without that guard pier, particularly when the wind is blowing from the south and south-west, the waters become so disturbed that the elevating of wheat becomes very- difficult.
Now, I wish to show that the particular attention of parliament should be directed, not for the purpose of constructing railways, but for the purpose of putting the waterways in the very best condition. It is well known to those Who have given consideration to this question that the waterway, no matter how inefficient, has a very large control over the rates charged by the railways during the open season. The lowest rates in the world for carrying wheat to-day are the charges front Chicago to New York. And What is the reason of

that ? Tlie reason is that the lowest charges by waterway are the charges by water from Chicago to New York.	The best
equipped railways in the world to-day are the railways from Chicago to New York, the reason being that the waterway adjoining has forced the railways to improve in this respect. Twenty years ago the curves on these roads were much more numerous and much more difficult than at the present time. The railways saw that, in competing with the waterways, they would be obliged to improve their means and methods. They straightened their curves, they lowered their grades, they increased the size and capacity of their ears, they increased the capacity of their engines ; and the consequence is that where, a few years ago, they could carry only from twenty-five to thirty cars, now they draw forty, and even fifty cars. This is owing to the improvements that I have spoken of. And, as I say, these improvements have been forced by the proximity of the waterway upon wlioise bosom floats tlie vessels of commerce. This shows us the importance of putting our waterways in a condition to control the railway rates in our own country. Another thing that we must bear iu mind is that the western states, in order to control the railway rates, seek an outlet at some place on the waterway. And as soon as they strike that point they can control the railway rates, because they can say to the railway : We will take the waterway unless you give us reasonable rates. The very best authorities in the United States who have investigated this matter agree on these points. No doubt lion, members will recollect, that in 1885, the Senate of the United States appointed a commission to investigate the transportation question. This is known in history as the Cul'lom Commission. Before this commission sat to hear evidence, they formulated questions which they sent out to men who were particularly well informed on this business, and one of these questions I will read to you. This question was sent out to ninety different individuals, for the purpose of ascertaining their opinion as to the controlling power of waterways over railway rates :
In making provision (or securing cheap transportation, is it or is it not important that the government should develop and maintain a system of water routes ?
The parties to whom this was sent included expert railroad men, steamboat men, engineers and others who had paid attention to these matters for many years. And of the ninety to whom the question was sent, seventy-three sent an answer to the following effect :
That a national system of water communication is the most certain and effective method of regulating railway rates and of insuring t.o the people the advantages of cheaper transportation.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Hon. members will probably remember reading the history of this committee and its report to the Senate. As a result of the findings of this committee, and based upon its report, a Bill was introduced and carried under which the Inter-state Railway Commission was appointed. I find in that report the following, which gives the opinion of the committee on this point of water communication, and shows the important effect of waterways upon railway rates in that country :
The evidence before the committee accords with the experience of all nations in recognizing the waterways as the most efficient cheapeners and regulators of railway rates. Their influence is not confined within the limits immediately accessible to water communication, but extends further and controls railroad rates at such remote and interior points as have not competing lines and the means of transport by water. Competition between railways, sooner or later, leads to combination or consolidation, but neither can prevail to secure unreasonable rates in the face of direct competition with free natural or artificial water routes. The conclusion of the committee is, therefore, that natural or artificial channels of communication by water

Now, note this :-
-when favourably located, adequately Improved and properly maintained, offer the cheapest method of long-distance transportation now known, and they must continue to exercise in the future, as they have invariably exercised in the past, an absolutely controlling and beneficial regulating Influence upon the charges made upon any and all means of transit.
Now, you will notice that there are three things as specified in this report as necessary. One is that the waterway Shall be favourably located. We have a favourable location ; we have a far more favourable location than the United States. The United States waterway is not to be compared with the Canadian waterway. For instance, they have one mile of canal for every four miles of open water; we have only one mile of canal for every sixteen miles of open water. They have only the Erie canal with its depth of seven feet, we have our canals with their depth of fourteen feet. We have rapid transit from Port Colborne to Montreal practically. It takes a barge on the Erie canal one month to make the round trip ; it does not take a week to make the round trip by our methods of transit. We are as near Liverpool at Hamilton as they are to Liverpool at New York. Montreal is 158 miles nearer to Chicago than New York is to Chicago. These are the advantages we possess. But they have a few advantages which we have not. They have no tolls upon the Erie canal, we have some tolls upon the Canadian canals. There is another advantage that we possess. The AYelland canal, on an average of twenty years, is open nineteen days longer in the season than the Erie canal. The La-chine canal is on an average open four days

longer than the Erie canal. Now from these facts you can see that our advantages are far In excess of those offered hy the Erie route ; therefore, other things being equal, we should be more than able to compete with the other route running through Buffalo to New York.
But there are disadvantages. They have better terminal facilities than we have. We have no facilities of any importance at Colborne compared with those at Buffalo. We have no elevators at Colborne elevating 40,000 or 50,000 an hour, as they have at Buffalo; therefore we cannot reasonably ex-pcct to handle the trade. They have elevators at Buffalo with a capacity of 21,-000,U00 bushels. They elevate grain at the small price of one-eighth of a cent per bushel. We have never done that, we have not been able to do it. It costs our people four times as much as that to elevate either at Colborne, or at Montreal; and can any reasonable man expect that Shippers and exporters, knowing these facts and these difficulties, will send their produce our way when they can get so much better facilities by other routes ?
Now let me point out the disadvantages under which the port of Montreal labours. Montreal is not a first-class harbour, it is not a second-class harbour, it is uot a fifth-class harbour. It is entirely deficient in facilities for handling the trade that might centre in Montreal. Therefore, it will be impossible for shippers and exporters to take advantage of that route when Montreal is in such a bad condition. I do not say that for the purpose of throwing cold water upon Montreal, because I consider that Montreal, if it had the proper equipment and apparatus, could handle the trade of this country, and that in less than twenty years its present population would be doubled or trebled. It is the gateway standing between the eastern and western trade. Our import trade must of necessity, if it comes by Canada at all, come through that door, and our export trade converging from the different points of the west must pass through the city of Montreal. Therefore, I have been of the opinion, that instead of waiting for private enterprise to put Montreal in a proper condition, it should be made a national port., the government should provide proper equipments at Montreal for that port to handle the trade of Canada. If that is done, rest assured that the trade will be largely diverted from other routes to Montreal on account of the natural facilities and advantages which that port possesses, and a large proportion of the trade now handled by the Americans will be handled by the Canadian people, and we will get the advantages of it.
Now, I want to give some facts showing the lack of facilities at the port of Montreal. The way that cattle are handled in the port of Montreal has largely driven the export of cattle to the port of Boston. Boston is
one of those ports thoroughly equipped and prepared for handling the export of cattle. Let me give you an idea of how they use cattle in the city of Montreal when farmers send their cattle by that way. The cattle come in, say, on the Canadian Pacific Railway. They are run down to Iloclielega where they are untrucked, and where they are fed, watered and rested, and that is proper. Then when the ship upon which they are to be sent across is ready, they are retrucked and run back to the point nearest to the ship, and that very frequently is 100 or 150 yards away from the ship. Then they are run down a steep gangway on to the platform of the wharf, thence they are urged along a narrow way between merchandise on the right and merchandise on the left, till they get to the gates of the sheds. Then they are urged through the narrow doors of the sheds on the front, and out of the narrow doors at the back, and then forced by twisting their tails, by goading and whipping, on board the steamer. When the cattle get on board the steamer, they are excited, they are heated, they are bruised, and consequently they enter upon the voyage in that condition. Cattle exporters in this country, who have given the matter consideration, tell me that this treatment depreciates the value of each animal from $2 to $5. Taking the lowest figure, last year we exported 115,000 head of cattle, a loss of $2 each would mean *230,000 lost to the farmers of this country by the poor means which are afforded them to handle the cattle, and to put them on board vessels in the city of Montreal. Now, *230,000 would pay the interest on six or seven million dollars. It would be cheaper for the farmers of this country to borrow five or six million dollars to equip the port of Montreal for the proper export of cattle.
Then again, Montreal is not a good port to ship flour from, and that is one of the reasons why the Grand Trunk Railway carries nearly all its flour to Portland. Mr. Lond, who was a prominent official in the Grand Trunk Railway service, has stated that the cost of shipping flour in Montreal is so high that they are seeking another way of shipping. He says this :	We come
into the city of Montreal with a train load of flour, we have no place to put that flour. There are not sufficient storehouses, and consequently we have to allow our freight to lie upon the track until we get an opportunity of loading it directly from the train. The cars are so far away from the edge of the wharf that we have to employ drays and carts, and the consequence is that it costs us about *4 a car for unloading, whereas if we had proper facilities and a proper place we could unload for at least $2 a car. That probably comes out of the exporters' pockets in Montreal. But, do not hon. gentlemen see that the profit of the farmer is lessened in proportion to the expense which it takes to remove these diffi-

culties and to overcome them ? All that comes ultimately out of the pockets of the farmers of this country.
Now, let us take another article, that of lumber. We export lumber from the city of Montreal very largely. I think last year we exported about 336 million feet board measure. When a ship is expected by the agents of shippers In the city of Montreal, they telegraph to the lumber exporters up the river, and other places, to send their lumber forward because they expect the ship on a certain day. The lumbermen send down their lumber, some in barges and some by rail. Very frequently it occurs that when the lumber arrives at Montreal something has detained the ship, the ship is not in the harbour; and consequently they have no pilling wharfs there, and the cars have to remain there with the lumber on board until the ship arrives, it may be one, two, three or four days, in some instances. On the other hand, the barges which come down have to remain with the lumber on board until the ship arrives. Well, the railway charges $2 demurrage every day that the car remains, and the barges charge $10 a day demurrage for their retention in the canal or harbour. The steamboat company has to pay that in Montreal, but of course ultimately the expense all comes out of the freight. If they had not to pay this expense the cost of the freight would be less, and that amount ultimately comes out of the pocket of the producer. Therefore, it is a loss to the producers to have this condition of things prevail in the city of Montreal.
Now, how do they do in Boston in loading cattle ? Cars run right down to the sheds on the edge of the wharf. The ship is lying in her berth. There are level tramways running from the floor of the cars right to the hold of the ship. The cattle are urged along quietly and put into their stalls. In that way the city of Boston has been known all over the continent; in fact one-third of the cattle imported into Liverpool two years ago came from the city of Boston. Until we, as Canadians, put the port of Montreal in such a condition as that it is impossible for us to expect the trade to go there. Now, there is another point ; how about the elevating capacity in the city of Montreal ? There is one elevator owned by the Grand Trunk Railway Company, or, at least, used by the Grand Trunk Railway. It is situated upon the canal where it cannot be reached by an ocean vessel at all. The other is operated by the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. I think, together, their capacity is 2,000,000 bushels. Now, how do they load ships ? Just let us look at that for a moment. They load the ships exactly as they did twenty-five years ago. They load the ships just as if the world were not moving forward at all. They have uie same equipment in the city of Montreal to-day as they had twenty-five Mr. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
years ago. They have the old exploded system of floating elevators. A barge goes to the elevator, gets a load then floats down to the vessel, and the load is transferred to the vessel at the rate of 4,000 bushels per hour. The best business that they ever did in the city of Montreal was loading the steamer Montcalm with 100,000 bushels in twenty-six hours. In the first year of the twentieth century, think of them loading in the city of Montreal at the rate of 4,000 bushels per hour, while at Duluth last year, they loaded a vessel at the rate of 193,000 bushels in 153 minutes. Do you really suppose that you can expect trade to go to the city of Montreal and wait to be loaded at the rate of 4,000 bushels per hour, and when we are so far behind in adopting the most recent inventions for expediting the transfer of freight to vessels ? It is impossible that any reasonable man can expect it. If we expect to do business in Montreal we must equip that port for the purpose of doing business as well as other ports are equipped. If not, do you expect to get trade ? How could you expect that the trade of Buffalo could toe diverted to Montreal when shippers know the conditions existing at one port and at the other ? At Buffalo 50,000 bushels of grain are elevated in an hour, and at Montreal 4.000 bushels are elevated in an hour. Do you suppose the shippers would be foolish enough to send their grain down to Montreal and pay half a cent a bushel for elevating it there, when they can get it elevated in Buffalo for one-eighth of a cent a bushel V Let us make our port a fraction of a cent cheaper than any other, and we will have the trade just as sure as we are existing, because the other conditions in Canada are far superior to those elsewhere. Now, I am going to give another instance. One of the Hamburg-American vessels came into Portland two years ago to be loaded from Grand Trunk Railway cars. Prom the time the vessel came in, was unloaded, and was reloaded with 265,000 bushels of grain and ten car-loads of other freight, only three days elapsed. Do you really suppose that the Grand Trunk Railway Company are wrong in seeking a port where their goods can be handled with such despatch allowing their trains to return to do business again ? If we want to get the Grand Trunk Railway business in Montreal, we will have to do better than we have been doing. Let me give a few figures which will probably astonish some hon. gentlemen. These figures are authentic. They are in regard to the congestion of trade in the port of Montreal during the season of 1897-8. On October 11, 1897, there were 447 cars lying on the sidings in the city of Montreal waiting for accommodation to be unloaded ; on November 2. 1897, there were 473 cars ; November 9, 451 cars ; November 10, 438 cars ; November 15. 427 cars ; or an average during these mouths of 464 cars

standing idle waiting for the accommodation which should be there to receive their freight as soon as they come in. Do you really suppose in ordinary business that if there were such congestion of trade as that, or that if any of you hon. gentlemen were wishing to transport your products, knowing these conditions to exist, you would send your goods forward to be exported from that congested centre ? I do not think you would. Taking the whole season from the opening of navigation in the spring until the closing in the fall, there were 315 cars on a daily average lying in that city waiting to be accommodated at the elevators, or on the wharfs. Let me give you a few more figures to show that the figures I have already quoted do not have reference to a special season or to special conditions. In May and .June, 189S, the Grand Trunk Railway had more than 1,000 cars upon the tracks waiting for accommodation, and the Canadian Pacific Railway about 500. On May 12, 1898, there were 439 cars waiting for accommodation ; on May 18, 314 cars ; on May 30, 532 cars ; on June 15. 446 cars ; and on June 17, 181 cars at Point St. Charles, and 423 were standing around the elevators without receiving the accommodation they desired. Now, I think I have said enough to show the House that while we express surprise that after all we have done we are not getting the trade for the port of Montreal, we can see the reason for this. We have deep canals and deep water, but this is a link in the same transportation route. The strongest part of the chain is the weakest link in it, and the strongest part of this transportation chain is the city of Montreal, which is a very weak link indeed. What do I propose to do ? I am not speaking for the government, but I think I am speaking for a large proportion of the people of the west, and I think I am speaking for the whole country when I say that parliament should direct the government to assume the port of Montreal. and make it a national harbour. They should have plans drawn by the most expert engineers in the country upon a magnificent scale, and let them go on with a portion of the plan as we can find the money. Let them go on for five, ten. fifteen or twenty years with the improvement of the port of Montreal, and then we shall have a port there of which Canadians may be proud. By that time trade will be very largely diverted along the lines to which we now look, and our trade will have reaped the advantages it can never have unless such things are done. We cannot leave the improvement of such a large harbour as that to private enterprise, and therefore, it is the duty of the government, in my opinion. to spend money, if it requires $5,000,000 or $10,000,000 to complete that work. Ten million dollars of an expenditure simply means about $300,000 a year, and I have shown that on cattle alone there was a loss
of $230,000, and the loss coming from lumber, the shipment of flour and a hundred and one other things would be three times covered by the $300,000 which I believe the government will be called upon to pay annually for the equipment of that harbour. There is another thing about the city of Montreal, and perhaps I should not say so much in regard to Montreal in the presence of an hon. gentleman who is a representative of that city. I am sure that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Blckerdike) will endorse every word I say with regard to the condition of the Montreal harbour. The wharfs in Montreal are on too low a level. It is impossible to erect permanent sheds on them, because the sheds would be carried away when the ice moves, and the result is that the sheds along the docks are temporary structures, which have to be taken away in the fall, stored during the winter, and replaced when navigation opens. You will see there is a great loss of labour and of money in all this. If the wharfs were built on a higher level the freight sheds could be permanent structures and they could be enlarged to meet the requirements of the trade. In Boston and New York the trains move down along the centre of the sheds on the wharfs, and the merchandise is unloaded into different sections ; one section for Liverpool, one for Glasgow, one for London, and so on. Then, when a vessel comes to port her loading is quite a simple thing. We have no such arrangement at Montreal, and consequently the railway cars have to unload in the night time. According to the rules of the harbour commissioners, trains cannot unload from 7 o'clock in the morning until 7 o'clock at night, because the general traffic occupies the space during the daytime. The consequence is that at 7 o'clock in the morning if a ship is not loaded and the cars are not unloaded, the train has to draw out and remain there for 12 hours before they can resume their work. It can very well be seen, therefore, that, as I said in my opening remarks, Montreal is not a first-class harbour, nor even a fifth-class harbour. I do not believe that you will find on the Atlantic coast any harbour worthy of the name which is so much behind the age as is the harbour of Montreal. Another reason why importers do not do their business through Montreal is this : When a vessel arrives, there is very frequently no cover for the merchandise she brings, and cement and tin and wire, and such goods are exposed to the weather and very often injured, notwithstanding that sometimes tarpaulins are used for covering. The importers who bring such goods into the country, and whose goods have been damaged will certainly not use that port again, but will seek some other, where the accommodation is better. In view of all this, would it not be wise for us all, irrespective of political parties ; would it not be judicious for us as Canadians to put the

port of Montreal In such first-class shape that it will accommodate the trade that we are soliciting. The federal government of the United States consider New York as a national harbour. They look upon it as the centre towards which a large portion of the western trade converges, and they have given about $10,000,000 towards the construction of piers, warehouses, and other works at that port. In like manner the United States federal government recognizes Boston as a national harbour, and they have made a grant of $5,000,000 to it, and so with Galveston, and so with many other ports on the Atlantic coast. Look at the port of Liverpool. One hundred years ago the annual trade of that port was only 500,000 tons, but the yearly trade of Liverpool today is over 11,000,000 tons. What is the reason for this vast increase in the trade of that port ? I will tell you. Liverpool, during the last 100 years has spent $100,000,000 on its port, or at the rate of $1,000,000 a year. Hamburg has spent $34,000,000 during the last twelve years, and many other cities in the old country as well as the new, have been spending large sums upon their harbours. Indeed, we might say that this is not an expenditure at all, but it should be viewed in the light of being simply an investment of money in the interest of the people. In Canada we would pay 3 per cent for the money expended on our harbours, and we would realize not 3 per cent but five times 3 per cent, which comes back to the people ; maybe not in the form of a few cents which we can see, but in the form of increased trade, increased credit, and increased development of our country in the various avenues of our greatness. I, therefore, believe that the government should make Montreal one of the best harbours ou the continent. Montreal cannot be considered as being a competing port unless we make such improvements as will enable us to compete. We cannot to-day handle the traffic as quickly or as cheaply as can other ports that have modern equipment. We must have such facilities as will enable a vessel carrying 80,000 or 100,000 bushels to have her cargo elevated in two hours and the vessel ready to resume her return journey. It has been said that a great difficulty is that we cannot get sufficient return cargoes for Canadian ports. Well, Sir, my opinion is that when we have our transportation system in proper shape and when exporters find it profitable to send their goods from our Canadian ports, then the merchants in Chicago, Duluth, Superior City, Winnipeg and other places west will import their goods through Canadian ports. The time will come when our trade will increase in the import line as well as in the export line, and when we have modern facilities in Canada the goods that now come to New York and Boston will come through Montreal or Quebec or Halifax or St. John, and be handled by the Canadian people to their advantage.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Now, there is also the question of the navigation below Montreal which must be attended to. My hon. friend from West Quebec (Hon. Mr. Dobell) pointed out the weaknesses there. We have an artificial ship channel, and that channel is not sufficiently wide, nor are there a sufficient number of navigation lights. There are jutting rocks which have to be removed and there are curves which have to be straightened, and with all these improvements made the insurance would be less and a large proportion of our trade would find its outlet by the St. Lawrence. I do not know of auy other subject which could better or more profitably be discussed by the members of this parliament. There is no question more interesting to the people of Canada, because our great fertile plains are so far removed from the seaboard that the question of cheap transportation to the markets of the world must ever be one of great concern to us. We cannot increase the price of our products, but we can so lower the rates of transportation that the producer will get the benefit, which will encliance the value of his products to him. I have deemed it my duty to place these facts before the House, because I have taken considerable pains to obtain them. I twice went to Montreal and I examined the port that I might be able to deal with this question intelligently, and for that reason I thought it advisable to present my views on this question in a 11011-political light. I say that both political parties are deeply interested in accomplishing this great aim in the interest of our country, and I trust we will all be able to move hand and hand towards success in that direction.
Can the hon. gentleman (Mr. Macdonald)' tell the House how much money the government has spent in improving the harbour of Montreal in the past ?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Up to last year, I believe, there has not been one single dollar spent by the Dominion government. True, they loaned money to the harbour commissioners for which they receive interest ; but they have never spent independently on the port of Montreal one dollar. so far as I know, unless they have spent it since the last session of parliament.

Mr. Speaker, I have listened with very much interest to the discussion which went on yesterday afternoon in this House, and the discussion which has been going on this afternoon, on the transportation question. The proper solution of that question will result in great benefits to the people of this country. I am a great believer in water transportation, in regard to which we have advantages in Canada which no other country in the world possesses. We have a natural system of water communication ex-

tending into the very heart ot this continent, 2,000 miles from the Straits of Belle Isle ; and what the government of days gone by, as well as the present government, have been trying to do is to make that whole system navigable for vessels of 14 feet draught, of 22 feet draught, of 2S feet draught, Therefore, I have no hesitation in saying that I support the policy of the present government in going ahead and deepening the St. Lawrence canals to 14 feet. In the discussion of this question, I fear that it will be impossible for me to avoid criticising the government for some things which they have done in connection with what I may term their transportation policy ; but I desire to say at the outset, that it is not a studied criticism, and I am sure they will receive it in the spirit in which I give it.
On the motion which is before the House. I suppose we may reasonably consider the transportation question not only as it affects the great railways of this country, but as it affects the fresh water navigation and the salt water navigation. I was very much interested yesterday, or the day before, in the Railway Committee, in hearing a note of alarm sounded by the hon. Minister of Railways (Hon. Mr. Blair) in reference to the action of the Grand Trunk Railway in transferring Its terminus to Portland from a Canadian port, in which we had all taken great interest, which we had been trying to build up in the hope that it would ultimately rival the port of New York. Some years ago the hon. Minister of Public Works (Hon. Mr. Tarte) said he hoped to make Montreal the Buffalo of Canada. I also recall a letter which the hon. Minister of Public Works wrote a few days ago to the president of the Montreal Board of Trade, in which he expressed alarm at the position in which we found ourselves owing to the Grand Trunk having transferred its terminus from Montreal to Portland. The government of the last four years have made rather loud professions in regard to their transportation policy, and, therefore. I think it is fair to criticise what they have accomplished.
What we have been trying to accomplish in the last few years has been to secure for Canadian channels the carrying of the products of Canada and their delivery at Canadian ports at the lowest possible cost. The question is, how far have we succeeded in accomplishing this ? In connection with the transfer of the terminus of the Grand Trunk to Portland and the diversion of the business which should go to Montreal, I desire to refer to a matter which has already been very thoroughly discussed in this House ; that is, the agreement which the government made with the Grand Trunk Railway for bringing the terminus of the Intercolonial Railway to Montreal. I would like to point out that Mr. Hoys, who was at that time the general manager of the Grand 35
Trunk Railway, stated plainly and publicly, before the agreement was consummated, that it was his intention to carry out the policy which the Grand Trunk are now about to put into effect, of making Portland their terminus in the summer as well as winter seasons instead of Montreal. In a speech which he delivered in Portland in the year 1898, and which was reported in the public press, he made that statement. In this connection I would also direct the attention of the House to the following figures. The total amount contributed by the present government towards the reconstruction of the Victoria bridge was $500,000. The amount paid annually by the government for the use of the bridge is $40,000 ; the amount paid annually for the use of the track from Ste. Rosalie to St. Lambert is $37,000 ; and the amount paid annually for the use of the Grand Trunk terminals at Montreal is $62,000. I have come to believe that owing to the great liberality of this government to the Grand Trunk Railway, that company have been enabled to use the money paid by the government for these purposes, in obtaining communication with Portland all the year round ; and my contention is that as this agreement was not consummated at that time, it would have been fair for the government to have said to the Grand Trunk : If you intend to do what your general manager says, the people of this country will not put up with it, and we must insert in the agreement a clause prohibiting you from going to Portland, and passing by the port of Montreal in the summer season.
A good deal has been said here this afternoon about the difficulties of transferring freight from railways to steamships at Montreal, and there is a good deal of truth in what has been said. At the same time, we must not forget that the Grand Trunk Railway Company have spent an enormous sum of money at Portland in the last few years ; and I think it would have been fair to have said to the Grand Trunk Railway, as a business proposition : You spend so much and we will spend so much on Montreal harbour ; you are the great gatherers of freight in the country, and especially in Ontario; you are the people who control the commercial arteries of this country; you control the lines of traffic which carry the produce, and we cannot and will not submit to your making Portland your terminus to the detriment of a Canadian port during the season of open navigation of the St. Lawrence.
In this connection I would like to draw the attention of the House to the number of miles of railway which the Grand Trunk own in this country. They own 3.194 miles, of which 2,600 miles, or about 80 per cent, are in the province of Ontario. As this House knows, the province of Ontario is gridironed with lines of the Grand Trunk Railway, and the exports of this country



are gathered by this railway and are taken to the various ports for export.
It cannot be denied that the rates of freight which the Grand Trunk Kailway collect for the transportation of this business are of a character sometimes described as burdensome to the producer, and I think that in consideration of the great fa\ ours which the Grand Trunk Railway have received at the hands of this administration and of previous administrations, and the great amount of Canadian traffic they carry, they are not treating the country fairly. The government, I think, could have prevented this. It is a cold and heartless proposition to come from the Grand Trunk Railway. This company practically say : We will pass through the city limits of Montreal and carry freight to Portland, a greater distance by 300 miles, at the same rate as to 'Montreal. I hope that the Minister of Railways and Canals and the Minister of Public Works will not content themselves with merely protesting against this but find some way of effectively checking it. For what does it mean ? It means that by the great influence which this corporation can wield over steamship companies, steamship after steamship will be driven away from Montreal, and we find that although last year the great Dominion Steamship Company declined to make Portland its port, in the summer season, this year it has had to bow to the inevitable. What now is the policy of the Grand Trunk Railway 7 In 1899, they made arrangements with the Reford line for a service to London from Portland ; in 1900, they made arrangements with the Thomson line for a similar service; and in 1901, they have arranged with the Thomson line for a service to London from Portland. In 1901 also they will have taken the whole fleet of the Dominion Steamship Company from Montreal, and I am informed on good authority that they are engaging with a company which now runs to Montreal, to run a steamship service from Portland to Glasgow. I am further informed that it is likely that, in 1902, they will have a Bristol summer service from Portland, and expect to have a service to Antwerp and Hamburg also during the summer. Where are the steamships to be engaged in those services to be taken from ? From Montreal, and instead of the St. Lawrence route becoming more popular, instead of our building up business over that route, and utilizing the great expenditure on our canals, we will find business being diverted to Portland, and we will have to spend enormous sums to get the steamship companies to come back again. We ought to deal with tins question very soon before any more steamship companies are engaged to go to Portland and give up the port of Montreal.
I wish to refer to our canal system. 1 believe that the government was justified in spending sufficient money to give fourteen feet draught to the St. Lawrence canals.
I put a question a few days ago upon the Order paper with reference to the depth of water in the St. Lawrence channels and canals between Lake Ontario and Montreal, and the reply of the Minister of Railways seemed to indicate that some transportation companies have been trying to depreciate our canals in the eyes of the public. I am not in sympathy with any such tactics. I believe that the railway companies perhaps in yeai's gene by tried to curtail the expenditui'e on those canals. The question I asked was : When does the government expect that vessels of fourteen feet draught will be able to pass from Bake Ontario through the carals and St. Lawrence channels to Montreal without lightei'ing ? And the reply of the minister seemed to indicate that we had that depth of water last season. We had the assurance of the Minister of Railways and Canals that there is foux-teen feet depth of water on the mitre sills in the canals, but the infox'mation which I had previously, and which I have obtained since, is that you cannot get foui'teen feet of water in the St. Lawrence channels except when the wind blows in a favourable direction. If the wind blows from tlie east, you cannot get more than twelve feet or eleven feet and one-half. This is a matter which ought to be looked into. 1 am not stating this for tlie purpose of criticising the government, but simply to assure the government that if it be necessary to spend more money in order to complete tlie channels, I will support it in that expenditure.
I noticed a report a few days ago that four large steamers wei'e being prepared in Chicago to go to Eui'ope by the St. Law-l-ence straight through without transhipment. These steamers are intended to take perishable products in cold stoi'age and also lumber and iron, and steel manufactures, and they prefer the northern route rather than that via New York. This is an experiment and is based on the belief that there is a depth of fourteen feet of water along the St. Lawrence route. Would we not be in a peculiar position, if, when those vessels reach the canals, after passing through the first canal, they should find the wind blowing from the east and have a wait over in the channel until the water rose ?
Let me draw the attention of the Minister of Railways and Canals to an article which appeared in the press on this subject, written by a very reputable gentleman, Captain Thomas Donnelly. I shall not take up time by reading tlie letter, but he stakes his reputation on the facts and accuracy of of statements he makes.
If these steamers can go straight through to Europe with the produce of the United States, it is fair to assume that we might reasonably hope to work up a through service from Canadian points on the upper lakes. This problem of transportation is of immense interest to the people of our great North-west, from which we hope, in a few

years, to have a greatly Increased export trade, and are therefore bound to open every avenue that will prove profitable to our farmers. But the province of Ontario is our great producing province, and it is in the interests of that province that the canals should be deepened to fourteen feet, and that we should encourage the building on the lakes of ships under the British flag, in which we are now very deficient.
We have discussed this question as regards the railways and the St. Lawrence canals, but 1 would like to draw attention to the fact that while a very large amount of money has been spent by the government on small harbours on the lakes, and while we have spent millions of dollars on improvements in Halifax and St. John

Hon. Mr. ROSS (Victoria, N.S.) There have been no improvements by the government in the harbour of Halifax because none are required.

I refer to the statements made in this House with regard to the amount of money spent for an elevator in Halifax and for improvements at St. John. Now, Sir, it may be an astonishing fact to the members of this House, but still the fact remains, that when the canals were eight feet deep the vessels that traversed them could come into Toronto harbour ; but, for years we have been trying to get a sum of money voted to take out of Toronto harbour the silt, the deposit of clay that has been flowing down a river from the country at the back and filling up that harbour. We have not been able to get that vote from the government. I hope, from the pressure that has been brought to bear and the explanations that have been laid before the government, that they will make' an adequate grant at this session of parliament in order to make Toronto harbour in depth the same standard as the St. Lawrence canals. Toronto is a great gathering point, it is the point in Ontario to which the freight comes from all directions; and we want to be placed in a position to take that freight down the St. Lawrence and out to the sea and deliver it at Montreal or Quebec if necessary, and so enable the farmers of Ontario to get cheap transportation.
I would like to draw the attention of the House while I am on my feet, to the importance of the shipments of freight from the city of Toronto. In the year 1898, there was occasion to get some facts made public, and these facts were then made public by the Grand Trunk Railway Company. They involve comparisons in freight traffic between Toronto and Montreal. I have no doubt that it will be surprising to this House to learn that Toronto is a greater shipping centre, notwithstanding that Montreal is a sea port, than Montreal is. In the month of January, 1898, the freight on the Grand Trunk Railway system from Toronto was 103,754 tons, against 58,091 j 35J
tons for Montreal. In the month of September, 1897, at a season when, it will be observed, Montreal has the benefit of ocean steamship traffic, the freight handled in Toronto was 105,000 tons, as against 9(5,000 in Montreal, while the passenger receipts for Toronto far exceeded those of Montreal. I would like my hon. friends from Montreal to understand that I give these figures, not to disparage Montreal, but to show how important it is to keep open this water communication and to equip Toronto harbour in a suitable way for this traffic. Something has been said about the various schemes that the government has in hand with regard to the transportation question. I think it was the hon. member for East Simcoe (Mr. Bennett) who stated that there were so many schemes on hand in connection with this matter that the public were somewhat confused. There is the Parry Sound Railway matter to which that hon. gentleman referred. I do not know that I can say that I ever heard the Minister of Railways (Mr. Blair) state that it was his intention to purchase the road on behalf of the government, but I think there was a discussion a year or two ago with respect to some remarks on that subject that fell from the lips of the hon. Minister of Public Works. Then there is the question, which has recently been resurrected, about the Georgian Bay canal, or the initiation of a project to improve the French river. Then, a year or two ago, the people of Port Hope sent a deputation here to interview the government and try to convince them that $8,500,000 could be save to the country in the Trent Valley canal scheme, if the terminus were made at Port Hope, instead of at the point intended on Lake Ontario. Then, there is the matter of Port Colborne to which I do not intend to give any time ; but I would like to have some one rise in this House and explain if it is not a fact that the improvement of Port Colborne was initiated to a great extent on account of a gentleman of the name of Conner, who expected to erect elevators at that point, and also had a scheme to improve the equipment of the harbour at Montreal. Were not the plans adopted largely under his supervision, and approved by him ? And now that this Conner syndicate is not materializing, 1 would like to know if it is the intention of the. government to go on and develop that scheme also. We have also another difficult question before us. and that is the matter of a Canadian marine on the lakes. We are at present, to some extent, in an experimental stage ; and the great difficulty is that we have not Canadian bottoms on the lakes, but the ships are all mainly those under the American flag. I would like to have the government propound some policy whereby we might encourage the building of a Canadian marine on the lakes. I believe it will bring great prosperity to this j country. And, in considering the trans-

portation question, and all these various routes, I hope the government of the day will take Into consideration this fact, that we cannot bring influence to bear in regard to water transportation to the same extent that influence can be brought to bear through the transportation companies who own and run railways, companies that represent an existing and fully established interest. If we could get more capital invested in a lake marine, we should be able to start the ball rolling, and should have a constant influence in the direction of improvements in water transportation, and the question would be raised to a position of importance equal with that which it holds in the United States. And further-in considering all these questions, I hope the government will not forget the part of the country (the province of Ontario) where the great volume of our exports is produced, and will not forget the importance, in any scheme they may have of interesting centres of population, for instance, Toronto, Kingston, Montreal and Quebec. If you [DOT]can get these centres of (population interested in any project, in the nature of things, that project will attain all the greater importance. I have to thank the House for the very kind attention with which they have listened to my remarks.

It will be expected, I presume, that, as the minister chiefly responsible for the canal system and its operation, I should have a word or two, at least, to say upon this subject before the conclusion of the debate, and I choose the present as likely to be the only opportunity that may offer, in the event of the debate concluding this evening. At the outset I wish to express to you, Mr. Speaker (Mr. Macdonald, Huron), the obligation which, I think is generally felt in the House, and which I certainly feel, for the very interesting contribution that you have made to the present discussion. We certainy got from you information, which, no doubt, had been collected with a very great deal of labour, information exceedingly valuable in itself, and tending to raise the discussion upon this occasion to a distinctly higher plane than that upon which, I am sorry to say, it had been placed.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS (Hon. A. G. Blair).

speechtext: Oh, oh.

I say that because both the hon. gentleman who made this motion (Mr. Bennett) and the hon. member for East York (Mr. Maclean), while disclaiming the slightest intention of giving the discussion any party political character, and while declaring that the question was one of a nonpartisan character and should be so treated, did not fail to devote a very considerable portion of the time they occupied to criticising from a party point of view and censuring in a party political sense, not only my [DOT] Mr. KEMP.
own acts and my own alleged omissions, but the acts and the alleged omissions of my colleagues. And I am sorry to have to acknowledge that my hon. friend from Toronto (Mr. Kemp), who has just taken his seat, has also sinned very notably in this direction. Let me refer at the very outset to what my hon. friend from Toronto has just spoken of. As I say, I am compelled to make reference to these matters, but would have very much preferred if we could have dealt with this question upon general principles, and dealt with it in something of a broad way, rather than that I should be compelled to answer statements and criticisms which are really beside the question, and which are practically of no interest or importance to the people of this country.
is'ow, one of these sinners is my hon. friend who has just resumed his seat. He thought it would be appropriate to drag in the arrangement that was made between the government and the Grand Trunk Railway Company when we took over the Drummond line and arranged for the extension of the Intercolonial Railway into Montreal. I cannot, Mr. Speaker, for the life of me, understand how the carrying of the business of the Grand Trunk Railway to Montreal was either encouraged, or promoted, or could have been prevented in any way by that transaction. The acquisition of the rights which were obtained by the government in the interest of the Intercolonial Railway from the Grand Trunk Railway, was an acquisition of interests and rights which were secured, because it was felt that they would be immensely to the advantage of the government railway. We paid no more than we believed they wei'e worth; we paid no more than we are sure the experience of the future will show that they are worth. We treated with them upon a distinctly business basis; and I think we would have been laughed to scorn, I know we would have been ridiculed by the Grand Trunk Railway people if, wheu we were offering to give them less than they were claiming, and no more than the privileges were worth, we should have attempted to annex some condition such as the hon. gentleman suggests; If, when we acquired from them the right of running our railway over their line from Ste. Rosalie to Montreal, and using their terminals, paying, I say, no more than those privileges were worth, they should have been asked to contract on their part to withdraw from the port of Portland.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I think you paid them less than they asked.

Now, my hon. friend will not deflect me from the course of my argument by making so entirely an immature and so inappropriate a suggestion as that. My hon. friend is an intelligent gentleman, one of the most intelligent on that side of the [DOT] House, and he knows that there is nothing

in tlie suggestion that lie now makes. My hon. friend (Mr. Kemp) asks this House to believe and to credit him with believing that in making a business transaction with the Grand Trunk Railway Company-when we were making no gift to them understand, when we were giving them no bonus, but simply paying them a moderate and reasonable price for valuable concessions-we should have attempted to make it a condition that they should withdraw from the harbour of Portland, and cease to make Portland a terminus of their line. Why, Sir, Portland has been a terminus of the Grand Trunk Railway since the line was first completed.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I referred to the summer traffic, not to the winter traffic taken to Portland.

My hon. friend says he refers to the summer traffic. Well, if we had attached any such condition as respects traffic in any portion of the year, the Grand Trunk Railway would never have entertained the proposition, and as a result we would not have been able to have made any arrangement with them for securing an entrance into the city of Montreal, and we would not have been able to make that arrangement which, outside of a few red hot and extreme opponents, is approved by the judgment and common sense of the people'of this whole country.
Now, Mr. Speaker, the hon. gentleman makes it a ground of criticism against us that we did not do as he suggests we might have done. If the hon. gentleman wants to make a political question out of it, I would ask him to consider the conduct of his own party and of his own government whose policy he has uniformly sustained. I would ask him to carry back his recollection to 1884, when the government of Canada was making, not a business arrangement, but practically giving a bonus of thirty million dollars to the great Canadian Pacific Railway corporation. A modest suggestion was made .to the government and to parliament at that time, that the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, in consideration' . of their receiving so munificent a grant from the exchequer of this country, should bind themselves not to expend any portion of the money that they were receiving as a gratuity from the people of Canada, in building up or creating a terminus or termini for their railway in any foreign country. How was that proposition received by the gentlemen whom my hon. friend is associated with, and by the government which he, during Its life, continued to support ? It was treated with absolute contempt, the proposition was voted down, received no sort of favour from the friends of the hon. member.
