Eleven million acres would furnish 10,000 acres per mile for 900 miles, making a total of 9,000,000, and furnish about 2,000,000 acres more for the three-tenths of the road of the eastern section, which the company were required to build within the first three years. So that within three years, the company should have acquired and obtained possession of the two twenty-four mile belts in the prairie section.
Now, I do not propose to .go any further into the speeches delivered at that time upon the contract, but I want to place in the witnessJbox another very important witness, and I am satisfied that the testimony of that witness will be accepted as being very important by the House to-nliglit. I want to put the Canadian Pacific Railway Company inlto the witness-box, and find out What they thought in regard to this land grant. I took the troube last year to borrow from the Deputy Minister of Railways and Canals the reports printed by the Canadian Pacific Railway, from the time of the inception of the syndicate. I went very carefully through all these reports, and I found some important statements made therein. The first report of the company was dated the 12th of December, 1882. Mark the date. Sir, December 12, 1882, shortly after the ratification of the contract:
The proceeds of the $20,000,000 of land grant bonds, as sold, are deposited with the government, which pays interest on such deposits at the rate of 4 per cent per annum.
I started out with the proposition that this
25.000.	000 acre land grant was available to the company from the date of the ratification of that contract. To-day we find that on the 12th December, 1882, they had sold land grant bonds, and that they had raised
820.000.	000 on mortgage. Surely we are not to be met with the argument of vested rights when we find that the company have had all the use of the land grant that they could possibly desire. Then the statement proceeds :
These proceeds are paid to the company in agreed mileage proportions (in the same manner as the government cash subsidy), as construction progresses ; and the balance of these proceeds and of cash subsidy coming to the company amounts to about $31,500,000.
I will now read from the report published by the company on the 31st December, 1883 :
A statement of land sales from the commencement of the company's operations, is also submitted.

It will be observed that a considerable reduction is shown in the acreage sold, as compared with the statement published in the official memorandum, dated December 12, 1882.
This has been caused, mainly, by a reduction of the acreage originally sold to the Canada North-west Land Company, from 5,000,000 acres to 2,200,000 acres.
The point I wish to make is that before the 31st December, 1883, the Canadian Pacific Railway Company had sold to the Canada North-west Land Company some 5,000,000 acres of land. Although you will find by the public records that the company did not have that amount of land set apart for them, ait that time ithey seemed to have been able to transfer any portion that they desired whether it had been set apart or not. Let me quote briefly from the Canadian Pacific Railway report of 1884, signed by George Stephen. He was asking for certain legislation from parliament to enable the company to do certain things, and he says :
Should this measure become law the position the company will occupy on the opening of the through line next spring may be summed up as follows :-*	.
It will have a cash deposit in the hands of the Dominion government sufficient to pay semiannual dividends at the rate of 3 per cent per annum on its $65,000,000 capital stock for seven and a half years, or until the end of the year 1893. It will own 3,299 miles, and will hold under lease 695 miles, of fully completed and thoroughly equipped railway, forming a total mileage of 3,994 miles. It will own more than 21,000,000 acres of agricultural lands.
We have the statement of President Stephen himself, that the company Will then have 21.000,000 acres of agricultural lands. In the report for 1885, we find this :
It will own three fine steel steamships on the great lakes, and an extensive and well-appointed telegraph system, with power to extend its telegraph linos to all parts of the country.
All this property, together with certain outside assets, in all valued at $230,960,585, will bo represented by a total indebtedness of $53,892,545, bearing an unusually low rate of interest ; and by $65,000,000 capital stock, for which dividends for seven and one-half years will be in hand.
Now, Mr. Speaker, if you will allow a diversion, I would like to refer to that matter. According to the president's own statement at that time they had set apart sufficient money to pay interest on the $65,000,000 of capital stock which the company had issued. You will find in the sessional papers a return made to parliament, in obedience to a request of the Hon. Edward Blake, in regard to that $65,000,000 of stock. That $65,000,000, in the then state of affairs of the company, they pretty generally admit was an unnecessary over-capitalization. The members of the syndicate distributed the stock among themselves at the rate of 25 cents on the dollar. They reserved a large quantity of the proceeds which were set aside to pay themselves dividends on this
MAT?OH 7, 1901
stock, and they actually paid tliemselves dividends at the rate of 6 per cent par value, or 24 per cent on the amount of money they had paid in.
Instead of turning the money in for the purpose of constructing the railway, they set it aside for the purpose of paying dividends on their stock at the rate of 24 per cent, so that in five years they had paid themselves more than they originally paid for the stock, and they owned the stock besides, and it was recently quoted at 102. Yet, Sir, we will probably be asked to-night to protect the vested interest of these stockholders. Well, when the House understands that these people pay themselves 24 per cent on this stock there will not be much sympathy felt for the vested interests of these gentlemen. I quote from the report of 1880 :
To represent this capital liability, the company has a well-equipped railway system of 4,651 miles, a thoroughly efficient commercial telegraph system, and nearly 15,000,000 acres of selected agricultural lands.
In 1880 they had nearly 15,000,000 acres and that was about the time the railway was completed. 1 think there is no hon. gentleman here who will not take the view that all the land became taxable at least at the time the railway was completed. I do not propose to weary the House with more than one other quotation, and that is the report of the company, dated the Sth May, 1889, which says :
In addition to the lands embraced in the foregoing statement, the company holds 1,389,424 acres of land in southern Manitoba, which came to it from the purchase of the Manitoba Southwestern Railway. These lands are among the best and most available in the North-west. At the average of the sales last year, $4.64 per acre, their value Is $5,944,785. They are subject only to a Hen of $884,773 in favour of the province of Manitoba. Your directors believe that they will yield at least $5 over and above the amount due to the province, and, as they are not liable to any other mortgage or lien, the surplus will be available to the general purposes of the company.
Therefore, according to the statement prepared on the authority of President Van Horne, the price the company received for their lands was $4.64 an acre, and he added that they would be worth and would sell for $5 an acre. But, take the price at $4.64, and we find that the subvention of lands to that company at 6,400 acres per mile was worth $32,100 per mile. I do not think that prairie roads cost more than $10,000 a mile, so that we practically gave to the company in lands alone three times the cost of the road, and yet we will be told that if we ask parliament to declare what parliament clearly meant, will be Interfering with vested rights. I could give further quotations from the statements submitted by the company, but I do not propose to go further into any technical argument on the question. I wish before concluding to point out that
the request which is made in this Bill is a reasonable and a just request. I remember that Mr. Blake in his speech quoted the statement of Sir John Macdonald when he was justifying the contract to parliament and where Sir John said : That by virtue of the vast subsidies which Canada was giving to this company it would be able to carry freight for at least one-quarter the cost that a road built out of private funds would be able to carry it for. In view of the fact that we gave that company $25,000,000 in cash, $35,000,000 worth of completed road, and $75,000,000 worth of land, it is only fair and reasonable to ask that that land grant should not be exempted from taxation in perpetuity. The greatest curse the North-west labours under at the present time is the exemption from taxation of these vast tracts of land, and the Minister of the Interior told us the other day that some 60,000,000 acres of laud had been given as subventions to railways in this country. 1 should think that at least 90 per cent of these lands are exempt from taxation. and parliament must see that it is handicapping that country for all time to come to continue this exemption. We have now a ciliance to set free about 20,000,000 acres of land and hon. gentlemen would understand what an immense relief this would be to the country. If parliament does its duty with regard to the Canadian Pacific Railway lands it will surely be expected to do its duty with regard to lands belonging to other railway companies. The Bill sets out in brief form some of the considerations I have mentioned, and it concludes with the following :-
Clause 16 of the contract mentioned in the preamble, between Her Majesty and the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, is hereby Interpreted to mean that the period of exemption from taxation of the said land grant terminated twenty years after the date of the ratification of the said contract.
I beg to move the second reading of the Bill, seconded by the hon. member for Alberta (Mr. Oliver).

This is a question which has already more than once engaged the attention of the House, and my hon. friend (Mr. Richardson) has just reminded us that last session we threshed it out at greater length than I care to do on this occasion. The hon. gentleman knows that the legislation against which he protests is contained in the original contract which the Liberal party of 20 years ago fought with all its might.
speakername: The PRIME MINISTER (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier).

speechtext: I said so.

Mr. Blake, who was then the leader of the party, opposed that contract with such vigour and ability as has never been equalled in this House. All the arguments which the hon. gentleman

(Mr. Richardson) has quoted to-day fell from the lips of Mir. Bliake and Mr. Ross and the other leaders of the Liberal party, upon a deaf House, and against the protests of those Liberal leaders this clause was put on the statute-book, lit was decreed that the lands conveyed to the Canadian Pacific Railway should be for 20 years exempted from taxation. There may be a difference of opinion as to the interpretation of the clause, but there can be no misinterpretation as to the meaning of ' twenty years.' The hon. gentleman (Mr. Richardson) has truly said that 1 20 years' means ' 20 years,' but the question is as to what date that 20 years should run. My hon. friend (Mr. Richardson) says that the 20 years should run from the date the contract was ratified, namely, when the Bill was passed, and he has quoted from the speeches made on that occasion to prove that such should be the interpretation of the contract. I wish it were so ; but, unfortunately, the language of the statute is very different from the language which was used in debate. The statute does not say, as my hon. frined will have it say, that the exemption of the said land grant shall terminate 20 years after the ratification of the said contract. If such had been the intention of parliament, it would have been very easy for parliament to have said so ; but that was not what parliament said. What parliament said was that these lands should be free from such taxation for 20 years after the grant thereof fi-om the Crown. I am sorry that it is so ; I wish it were otherwise ; but it cannot be argued seriously that the grant from the Crown was made at the time of the ratification of the contract. That is one reason.
But ther-e is another reason which my hon, friend has not alluded to, and which is very conclusive on this point. There was a contract entered into in 1880, between Her Majesty, represented by the government of Canada, and certain gentlemen-Canadian, Americans, Englishmen, Hollanders, and Frenchmen-who undertook to build a railway on Canadian soil. For this undertaking on their part the people of Canada agreed to give them $25,000,000 in cash and 25,000,000 acres in land. Did that grant operate and become valid so as to be exacted by the company on the day of ratification of the contract ? Quite the reverse. If on that day the Canadian Pacific Railway Company could have claimed their $25,000,000 of money and their 25,000,000 acres of land, there would be some reason for the contention of my hon. friend. But, on the contrary, the Act said positively, in so many words, that the grant would be available, not on that day. but at the time the subsidy would be earned by the building of the railway. Here is the clause :
In consideration of the premises, the government agree to grant to the company a subsidy in money of .$25,000,000 and in land of 25,000,000 acres, for which subsidies the construction of Sir WILFRID LAURIER.
the Canadian Pacific Railway shall be completed and the same shall be equipped, maintained and operated.
My hon. friend agrees with me, I am sure, that under the terms of this clause, the subsidy could not be paid to the company except as tbe construction of tbe road proceeded. It seems to me that Is quite clear without further argument.
It could not with regard to the money ; tout so far as the 'land is concerned, they borrowed money on it instantly.
Not instantly, but later on ; and if my hon. friend were to contend that the twenty-year period were to run from the day the company mortgaged the land, there would toe some argument for that.
Would the right hon. gentleman support me if I modified my Bill to that effect ?

I will not support the hon. gentleman when he asks parliament to interpret its own Acts. I said last year that my hon. friend could take the matter before the courts. He says that last year, when he made his argument, I called him a socialist. 1 said that his argument smacked of socialism, if it were not the pure article itself. In what other way could I characterize it ? Why should a contract be sacred, why care for the Bondholders, why not make the bondholders weep ? Because we are in a British country, and if there is anything held sacred in a British country, it is a contract. My hon. friend says, do not leave the courts to interpret the contract, tout put on it sucn interpretation as you hold. My hon. friend asks us to do something which has never yet been done in a British parliament. If there is anything which the British parliament has a horror of, it is to interfere with contracts. I regret that provision of this contract as much as my hon. friend does. He has argued that it is a serious blot oil our statute-book, that it is an injury to the settlement of the North-west. I agree with hinj that it is so ; yet, for my jjart, I am not prepared to say that the bond holders must bleed or weep, or to take away their property and their security from them. My hon. friend should not bring such a proposition before this House. I suggested to my hon. friend last year that he should go before the courts and get their interpretation of this contract. How, my hon. rriend asks, can this be done ?-the lands have not been patented. Well there are many thousands of acres which have been patented, on which the matter can be tested in the courts.
My hon. friend made another argument: he said that these municipalities are poor, and that this government might do this. If I understood the hon, gentleman's argu-

ment aright, he did not want any judicial interpretation. He said the meaning was too clear-we could interpret it ourselves.
That is my position.

If that is my hon. friend's position, it is a position against which I contend with all my might. If my hon. friend is sincere and earnest in this matter and wants to have it tested in the courts, I am here to tell him that the government will back him with all their might in so doing ; but, if my hon. friend says, 1 do not want a judicial interpretation, but I want parliament to say that the exemption started on such a day, whether we would rob the- bondholders or not, I am not prepared to assent to anything of the kind. The proposition I make to my hon. friend is a very reasonable one-to have a judicial interpretation, and we will give the poor men of those municipalities all the assistance we can in order to have their rights, whatever they are, established. If my hon. friend is satisfied with that, the government will assist him with all their power to have this contract judicially interpreted. But if he is not willing to accept that, and says there is nothing to do but to have parliament interfere and say whether it is right or wrong, whether it is according to the truth or not. that the twenty years must run from a certain day, then, I hope that such a monstrous proposition, such a socialistic proposition, will receive no countenance in this parliament ; and the only position I have to take is to move that the Bill be not now read a second time, but be read a second time this day six months.
I would ask the right hon. First Minister if the government would not state a case for the Supreme Court, and have the contract interpreted themselves V
I have just said that if it be the wish of the settlers of the North-west to have it interpreted, I will do so.
You said you would assist me in the matter. I ought not to be placed in the positon of having to take the initiative.

We have heard a lawyer's argument from the leader of the government and the great exponent of Liberalism in this House. Is there no other course than to refer this matter to the courts ? I say there is. We have had grievances of the people of the North-west brought before this House time after time. The greatest grievance the people of the North-west had was the monopoly clause in that contract, which prevented any other road than the Canadian Pacific Railway building to the American frontier. That grievance was aireu in this parliament, and eventually the Conservative party,
which put that monopoly on the country, found a way of removing that grievance. When the Canadian Pacific Railway came here for further concessions, it got them, but only on condition that it removed this grievance. The Canadian Pacific Railway has come to this House session after session, since hon. gentlemen opposite have been in office, asking fof favours, and I have always contended that we should take advantage of these applications to make terms on behalf of the North-west people.
The hon. Minister of Railways gave the Canadian Pacific Railway great concessions in connection with the Crow's Nest Pass Railway, and he obtained in return reduced freight rates for which he claimed great credit. Two years ago the Canadian Pacific Railway demanded further concessions, and got a blanket charter over the whole of the North-west. I then protested that then was the time to get rid of some of these monopolistic clauses in the contract, particularly the 10 per cent clause, which prevents this government from interfering with the freight rates until the company earns 10 per cent over its expenses, but 1 protested in vain. The Canadian Pacific Railway is asking again this session for further concessions, and hon. gentlemen opposite will, no doubt, be as supine as they were in the past. They have not the courage to insist on the removal of these monopolistic clauses. There are two such clauses remaining. One is the clause granting exemption from' taxes, and the other is the 10 per cent clause. Time and again attention has been drawn to these grievances by gentlemen from the Northwest, but all we can get is a lecture from the right hon. the Prime Minister on vested rights and the iniquity of interfering with them. But that is a lawyer's plea, and not that of a statesman. A statesman is a man who can take advantage of opportunities and always find a way to remedy grievances, but here we have Liberals going about the country before elections weeping for the farmers, and in parliament weeping for the bondholders.

I am sure my hon. friend does not want to give any more to the Canadian Pacific Railway than we have given. According to his contention, this monopoly is at an end, and the twenty years exemption have expired. If the courts maintain his view, why need we grant any further favours to the Canadian Pacific Railway in order to obtain this concession V

The right hon. gentleman has given a great many concessions to the Canadian Pacific Railway since he came into office, without obtaining any corresponding benefit from that company. The Canadian Pacific Railway is here this session asking further concessions, and the right hon. gentleman will have his opportunity of settling this disputed point and

obtaining something for the people in return for what he will give the company. But he will not take advantage of the opportunity. Instead we will have the lawyer's plea that vested rights are sacred, that contracts must he upheld, and not a word will we hear about the grievances of the people. But a statesman can find a way to remedy the grievances of the people, and at the same time do no injustice to vested rights.
Give us a way out of it.

I have two cures for it. The Canadian Pacific Railway came here some years ago and got a most valuable blanket franchise over the whole of Manitoba that had not already been pre-empted. Let us impose on them some conditions tills year in return for the favours they ask. The hon. the Minister of Railways (Hon. Mr. Blair) laid down last session the doctrine-and so did the hon. Minister of the Interior (Hon. Mr. Sifton), who is not here this evening-that the present administration was composed of statesmen who would get something for the people from great corporations in return for anything they gave. That was the whole justification advanced for the Crow's Nest Pass deal. The only justification was that the Canadian Pacific Railway was compelled to give up something in the way of monopoly.
I have another cure for the situation, and that is government ownership. We can get that railway, into our hands for a very small consideration, and we will get all these lands back.
Will you buy the lands back ?
No, if you buy the road you will get the land with it.
Not necessarily.

If you buy the shares you get everything the railway owns, and you get the lands back. There are very few lands left in the North-west now to give to the settlers, and the easiest remedy would be to acquire the Canadian Pacific Railway.
How much would it take to buy it ?

Mr. Shaughnessy has told you that you can get it absolutely for S3P.vo0.000. I believe you can get the control for less than $25,000,000. and there is enough land there to pay for all that. You can get that land back into the hands of the country. You could give it to the settler free. Or you could devote the proceeds of sales to paying the taxes and helping the settlers. Instead of spending our time talking about the great corporations, we should be doing something for the people. We should do away with this most unfair sys-Mr. MACLEAN.
tem of exemptions under which the poor man has to pay the piper. The poor man in Toronto and every little hamlet in Ontario, and all over Canada to-day, is paying the municipal taxes, while great corporations go scot free, which would not be the case much longer if Liberals would stand by their pledges. But they have gone back on their pledges, and to-day are defending the corporations and weeping for the bondholders. They only weep for the farmers when out in the country looking for their votes.
I believe that this wrong can be made right. As soon as I can get away from here, I intend going up to the North-west and telling the people there how this parliament regards a question of this kind, and I will let them know that the little Napoleon was not in his seat to-night when this question was being discussed, and that the young bucks from the plains, who talk so much about the people's rights on the public platform, are out to-night at some kind of a sun dance or corn dance.
Oh, oh.
That no doubt is great sport for hon. gentlemen on the other side.
Which one of the young bucks is at a sun dance ?
I see that some of them have come back from the sun dance.
Will the hon. gentleman uarne one who was absent ?

Now, it is very fine to hear these interruptions from the Northwest whenever a proposition in their interest is before the House. But, I want to tell hon. gentlemen opposite and to tell the Premier that there is a way to cure such evils as we complain of. He has availed himself of it once; he has failed to avail himself of it several times. He had better avail himself of it hereafter. For the people do see that parliament in this country is supreme, that parliament can rectify every wrong. And parliament does not rise to its responsibility if it does not find a way to right a known wrong. Law, we are told, is for the purpose of righting wrong; and, if there is no law, or if it is found that the law cannot right the wrong, this parliament can if it will but find a way. And some of us will find the way, and some of us will stake our reputations and our future on the finding of a way. I am one of those who will consecrate what strength I have and what effort I can put forth to that end. It is a strange thing to hear a Prime Minister of this country, a man who professes always to be a Liberal, throwing out some kind of insinuation against those of whom he speaks as socialists. I am something of a Socialist, and something of a Tory.
That is a bad mixture.

No, it is not. I am one of those who do not regard socialism as a crime. Somehow, the world is suffering under great grievances, and the men who profess to be socialists are men who are trying to do something for humanity. I belong to two or three clubs in this country, and some are rather exclusive. And when 1 go into those clubs, 1 hear the members talking about these socialist fellows on the hill here. 1 wish these gentlemen, and some hon. gentlemen opposite, who speak in this manner could be in some of the London clubs to-day. They should hear what is said in those clubs by men of great family connections, leaders in the universities of England, men high in the service of the state-and nine-tenths of these men are socialists, if you call them such. And the great city of London has set an example to the world in the last two or three days of what socialism on good lines means. The London County Council is taking over the control of the great utilities which, until now have been in the hands of private corporations who have been robbing the citizens of London right and left. Of all the robbing corporations, some of the very worst were the water companies that controlled the water supply. They are going out of existence. The city of London is taking over every tramway there. The state owns the telegraph and telephone services. The gas works and electric light works of the city of London are owned by the public. That is the kind of socialism I believe in, and I am not afraid to say so, even though I am opposed by gentlemen who profess to be Liberals. But, I hope that this is the last time that a Liberal Prime Minister in this country will say a word against socialism of that kind. Before I finish, let me say again that the responsibility rests upon parliament of righting this wrong of the Northwest settlers. That wrong may have been inflicted upon them by the Tory party. For that, the Tory party is responsible. But equally does the responsibility rest upon members of the other side as well as upon members on this side to right what is a wrong and to find a cure for what is a grievance.
The SOLICITOR	GENERAL (Hon.
Charles Fitzpatrick).	In 1S80, a contract
was entered into between the government of the Dominion of Canada and a certain corporation, under which the corporation undertook to build a railway extending from central Canada to the Pacific ocean. As a result of the making of that contract, certain grievances, apparently, have resulted to the people of the North-west Territories and Manitoba. Now. these grievances were pointed out by the Liberal party at that time as being the necessary and inevitable result of that contract. Since that time, this parliament has been asked, by means of the Bill now before the House for consideration, to remedy that grievance-that is to say, the hon. gentleman who presents this measure asks that the remedy be applied in this way. He says : The contract was made between the people of this country and a firm of contractors or a railway corporation, and we now ask you to undertake to construe that contract, and practically to set the contract at defiance. The government now in power says :	We do
not think it proper to consider the contract in that way. We do not think it proper that one of the parties to the contract should take it upon himself to construe the contract as against the other party, but this contract once made, should be left to the courts for judicial interpretation. And the hon. gentleman from East York (Mr. Maclean), who now leaves the House, says, the course adopted by the government is an improper course. He says :	It is all right
for lawyers to talk about the sanctity of contract and about respecting their obligations contracted under such conditions as those under which this contract was made, but we statesmen deal otherwise with these things. We statesmen, he says, take out our knives and put them through these contracts and put an end to them. It is all right for mere lawyers to talk about keeping sacred their covenants, but we statesmen deal otherwise.
Now, did I say that ?

Mr. Speaker, it seems to me, having stated the xiositioii taken by the hon. gentleman and by the government, the matter is at an end. We say :	The contract is made: in consequence
or as a result of this contract, certain obligations were entered into by the jieople of Canada towards the bondholders who made the advances necessary for the purpose of enabling this road to be built; and, if there is any doubt about the terms of this contract, let the courts settle it and put it at an end: but it is not proper for us to interfere and to construe this contract ourselves, violating obligations we have entered into towards these bondholders. Let me go one step further. What are the facts ? When this contract was entered into, it was provided that the road was to be built by the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. To enable the company to build that road certain grants of lands were to be made to the company as the road progressed. The company was authorized to use the land grant for the purpose of borrowing money, not only upon the land granted, but the lands to iie granted under this agreement. These bonds were sold, and the money for which they were sold was taken by the company and put into this road. And now we are asked to take that land grant which was made at that time and given to the bondholders as security for their advances, and to say that we are going to alter the con-

ditions under which the grant was made. Now, is that common honesty, Mr. Speaker?

Would the hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Fitzpatrick) allow me to ask him whether he would be willing to have this interpreted to mean that these lands shall be taxed twenty years from the date they were earned ?

I am not going to say how I should be willing to have this contract interpreted. If the hon. gentleman (Mr. Richardson) will try to understand the position the government takes, I am sure we shall be at one in a moment. The government say : The contract is made providing that these lands shall be exempt from taxation for twenty years after the grant thereof from the Crown. All that is necessary is to ask the courts to construe the words ' grant thereof from the Crown.'
Yes, but you have not issued the patents up to the present time.

Now let me go on. Are these words to be construed as of the date of the making of the contract, as my hon. friend wishes them to he construed ? Are they to be construed as of the date of the earning of the lands, or are they to be construed as of the dates when the patents issued ? These are the three constructions that may be put upon these terms : and what we say is that as these terms are vague and indefinite, and are possible of any one of these three constructions, let us refer the matter to the courts and let the courts construe them. If the court says that when this contract was made the meaning of these words was of the date of the making of the contract, then we have no responsibility. If the court decides that the grant is to be understood as of the date when the land grant was earned, we have no responsibility. If they say it is of the date when the patent issued, we are equally without responsibility.
Yes, you are responsible, because you have allowed five years to elapse, and you have not issued the patents.

It is for the courts to say the date from which that grant is to run. Now, any hon. frieud takes this position, he is endeavouring to tax the government with responsibility for not having granted patents during these five years. Why does he not bring in a Bill to discuss that question ? What we are dealing with now is the hon. gentleman's Bill ; I presume he drew it, and if he drew it, I presume he understands it. What the hon. gentleman wants to do is to say that this grant is to be construed as dating from the date of the ratification of the contract. That is what he asks us to do ; and I submit respectfully, Mr. Speaker, that we should not by an act

of this parliament say that such is the meaning of that contract and the Act that was based upon it ; and if there was a possibility of construing the contract in that way, then we must not forget that the land never passed out of the possession of the Crown until such time as the road was constructed and the grant earned.
It has not passed out of the possession of the Crown yet.
So the position is this : My hon. friend, if he is sincere about this matter-
Do you suppose I would be doing it if I were not sincere ?

if he is sincere about that matter, as sincere as the hon. member for Alberta (Mr. Oliver) was when he spoke on this subject last year, he would adopt the suggestion thrown out by the government, that is to say, he would have the contract referred to the courts and the courts, would judicially construe it. Then the people of the North-west would benefit by it, and no individual would succeed in obtaining some political benefit out of it. I say the position of the government takes is one which will commend itself to the House. Let there be a judicial construction put upon this contract, that is all any member can ask, then we will know where we are, and how far this evil complained of can be remedied.

SI'ROL'LE (East Grey). The hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Richardson) deserves credit for the anxiety he displays ou behalf of the people he represents. There is no doubt, people in Manitoba are labouring under a grievance, under a hardship, and there is no doubt they desire aud deserve a remedy, no matter from what quarter it may come. The hon. member brought this question up last year, and, if I remember right, he brought it up before that; but he has always aimed at redressing the grievance under which the people of Manitoba labour. But I regret to say, personally, that I cannot agree with him in the remedy he proposes. If there is one thing more than another that ought to be held sacred by parliament, it is the contracts that we make with corporations or individuals ; and there is no doubt that this was a contract that parliament entered into seriously and intentionally, whether it was a wise oue or not. We are one of the contracting parties, and to violate that contract by an arbitrary declaration, to make that Act mean what we desire it to mean, I think, would be entirely out of keeping with the principles usually obtaining in ail constitutionally-governed countries under the British Empire. The

hon. member for Lisgar quoted from several members of the Reform party, giving their interpretation of that Act when it was being passed, and amongst them he quoted from the Hon. Edward Blake. Now, it seems to me that Mr. Blake thought at that time that the twenty years were to run from the time when the agreement was entered into. That being the case, I respectfully submit that it justifies any person in holding a similar view, and the hon. member for Lisgar is not so much to blame if he comes to the same conclusion and desires to act on it. That was Mr. Blake's opinion, and that was the opinion of several members of the Reform party, but it does not happen to be the opinion of those who constitute the other contracting party.
When this question was up last year I made a suggestion which the 'First Minister has intimated he is willing to act upon tonight. I suggested that the government should state a case for the court to decide, instead of leaving it to any private individual to prosecute a case in court in order to secure the rights of the people interested.
I understand the First Minister to say tonight that he is willing to join with the hon. member for Lisgar, and to have a case stated for decision by the court in order to ascertain the correct interpretation of the law. It seems to me the hon. member for Lisgar should accept that offer. I do not think it is possible for him to secure any remedy that will redress this grievance at an earlier date ; and since the government have assumed responsibility and given their Solemn pledge in the House that they will act in this manner, I think that ought to be acceptable. The hon. member for East York (Mr. Maclean), I regret to say, stated some propositions that 1 cannot agree with. I cannot agree with him in the conclusion he reaches in regard to this and many other cases of a cognate character. He gave us an example of remedying a grievance suffered by the people of Manitoba and the North-west Territories some years ago with regard to the monopoly clause ; but he evidently forgot that we did not arbitrarily interpret that clause, but we entered into negotiations with the contracting parties that were controlling the situation, and induced them to abandon their rig-fits.
That is my proposal exactly, negotiate now respecting the lights in order to get rid of the grievance.

Well, if the hon. gentleman had only gone that far il should have been glad to support him ; but to say that we should arbitrarily interpret a law in a manner to suit our own side of the question, is going much too far.
I did not say that for a moment.

On the other hand, to say that parliament is above the people and
above the contracts, and that we should violate a solemn obligation we entered into with a corporation, I think is also going entirely too far. Now, had the government acted on this suggestion last year, they would have done right. They have agreed to what is, in my opinion, the only remedy, and I am sure the House will sustain the First Minister in that suggestion. Therefore, I think it will be the part of discretion, and it will be the honest way of securing a remedy, if the hon. member for Lisgar, who is entitled to great credit for the perseverance he has displayed in the interest of the people, would accept that suggestion and withdraw his Bill.

It seems to me this is a very simple question, and there has been a great deal of discussion wide of the mark by one or two hon. gentlemen who made long speeches. A great many matters that are not pertinent to the question were brought in. I think the House understood the hon. member for East York in the same way as the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) understood him. He, as an old parliamentarian, must know that he was entirely out of order, because his argument would have nothing to do with the question before the House. I am glad to hear that he did not mean anything like as drastic as he said and as we understood him.
Oh, no.

That is the way we all understood him. I will now leave it and say nothing more about it. The whole question is rather broader than the statement of it by the hon. Solicitor General (Mr, Fitzpatrick), In my opinion. The whole question is not the interpretation of the contract, but it is that we shall not interpret it at all. We have no business, as a House, or as a legislature, to put a construction on a contract that has been entered into.	.
I agree with that.

If you do agree with it, I do not think it is wise or fair in discussion to bring these other matters into contention for the reason that those hon. gentlemen who stick closely to the question, and -who argue it upon that line are placed in an unfair position, because in arguing a lot of other matters it would look as if those of us who are strong on this question are not standing up for the rights of the people. I am one of those that willingly will never consent to one tittle of that sort of legislation, because it is the bulwark of the poor man. The poor man is the man who most often requires the law to protect him within his rights. I grant there is no socialism about me as I understand socialism. There is no socialism about Conservatism, as I understand it;

otherwise, I would be beginning to think of becoming a Liberal, because I am glad to say that as far as I hare observed the legislation of this country, there is no record of the Liberal party being socialistic in their actions in parliament. We all, I think, agree upon that ; at all events, excepting the new members in the House, we all agree because we voted upon it last year. I was going to read a few words from the speech of Sir Charles Tupper, our then leader on this side of the House, but I do not think it is necessary. He endorsed entirely, I think, the words of the right lion. Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier), as he expressed himself last year, and I think all of the members of this side of the House endorsed him also. To-night, I believe that nearly all of us, I think probably every one would do the same, if the question came to a vote. As the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Richardson) quoted from some of the speeches and transactions which occurred at the time of the passing of this contract, there are one or two quotations that I will detain the House by referring to, for a minute or two, because I do not see the pertinency of the hon. gentleman's quotations any more than the pertinency of some of the things the hon. gentleman 'said. He quoted what Liberal members said in opposition to this contract at that time. He did not quote, as the Prime Minister has remarked, from these discussions one thing pertinent to the question, or that would help us in the consideration of it. As great a lawyer as Edward Blake would seem to have been satisfied with it. He left us in this dilemma as to what the contract does mean, because, I agree with the hon. Solicitor General and with the right hon. Prime Minister that it is doubtful what the construction is. But, the hon. member for Lisgar went on to speak as if the Liberals were all against the proposition. He forgets that the Hon. Alex. Mackenzie, while endeavouring to grapple with this question, made a much larger offer, an offer of 50,000,000 acres of land, $25,000,000 cash, and 4 per cent on whatever it might require beyond that, and asked for tenders upon that basis. So that the House will know that all the difficulties and all the extravagances, if there were extravagances in regard to the terms given by the Canadian Pacific Railway, were not upon our side of the House. The hon. gentleman read from the speech of the present Prime Minister of Ontario, but he forgot to read the recantation of that hon. gentleman. I will read it for his edification, because he ought to read what he said then, and what he says now. He was then dealing with a matter which was surrounded with difficulties, and which awaited the test of the future. He was in opposition to the proposition, because he then took the Liberal view of it. Mr. Ross, speaking in one of the constituencies in Ontario within a year past, said : Mr. TISDALE.
I remember when the Canadian Pacific Railway was constructed, we thought Sir John 'Macdonald was undertaking a herculean enterprise, one which would crush the country. I think, perhaps, he was right, and we were wrong. I think, perhaps, he budded more wisely than he knew. No one will say to-day that the building of the railway was a mistake. Canada today would be a very small country, would be weaker in the councils of the empire, would scarcely be a confederated Dominion, as it is, were it not for the Pacific Railway.
In discussing a matter such as this I would prefer that we should briug no party politics into it. I merely make reference to these two statements because the bon. gentleman saw fit to bring before the House, and to the attention of the Prime Minister, portions of the discussion which took place then, that seemed to be, from his standpoint, evidence that the action of the Conservative party in reference to this great enterprise, this herculean task, which was undertaken by the great man who is here no more to give us his counsel, has not verified the anticipations of those who projected it. I wanted to give the views of one of the strongest men who existed at that time, and who still gives his counsel, wisdom and best efforts to the province of Ontario. I would prefer, and I always endeavour to carry out that view in discussing matters like this, where there are no party politics, that we should deal with them simply on their merits as the right hon. gentleman has done to-night. In his speech a year ago he went into some other subjects. This is not a matter of party politics. It is one of those things where both parties should feel some of the difficulties and responsibilities, and unless it is a matter in which party politics are concerned. I think the wiser and better plan is to deal with the subject just as we have with this, and pitch into each other on party questions.

Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to go very far afield in the short remarks which I desire to make in regard to this subject, and I would not delay the House by participating in the debate at all, were it not that I think it is an extremely important subject, and it affects particularly that part of the country which I am supposed to represent in the cabinet. It is not by any means a new subject, as we all know, and it does not seem to me that it is a subject upon which there can be very much difference of opinion. I would be surprised if any member of the House of Commons of Canada would be found to take the position that this parliament would be justified in altering a contract which has been deliberately entered into. What certain members of parliament thought and said when this contract was passed, has absolutely nothing to do with the question. What this man or that man said as to the

intention of an Act of parliament lias nothing -whatever to do with the Act when it is passed. When a contract is made by this parliament with a corporation or individual, it makes no difference whether that corporation or individual turns out to be unpopular or not, that contract must stand absolutely. We have no more rights as a parliament to pass an Act interpreting that contract than you would have, Mr. Speaker, to place your own interpretation upon a contract that you might make with me in private life. For my part, I take most emphatic issue with the hon. member for East York (Mr. Maclean) when he says that the House of Commons is supreme in the sense that it has a right to break its contracts or violate public faith.
speakername: The MINISTER OF THE INTERIOR (Hon. Clifford Sifton).

speechtext: The member for East York did not say that, nor did not advocate it.
I think he spoke for the Bill.

I did not speak for the Bill.
The	MINISTER	OF	THE	INTERIOR.
The hon. gentleman (Mr. Maclean) is very unfortunate then in the language he used.

No, he is not.
The	MINISTER	OF	THE	INTERIOR.
The hon. gentleman told us, with great vigour, that parliament is supreme, and that parliament has the right and the power. We all know it has the legal power.

By concession for concession.
The	MINISTER	OF	THE	INTERIOR.If the	hon. gentleman	did not mean that
parliament had the power rightfully to alter contracts, then his remarks were totally irrelevant, and could not convey any intelligent idea to those who listened to him. The question was well and clearly put by my hon. friend the Solicitor General, and by my hon. friend from South Norfolk (Hon. Mr. Tisdale). It is not a question as to what Interpretation should be put on this contract. Parliament has no right to put any interpretation on this contract. The interpretation of a contract made betwen two parties must be decided by a judicial tribunal, independent of both parties. The hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Tisdale) said truly that if this course were taken, it is not so much the large corporations that would suffer in this country as the poorer classes, because the trend of legislation in all countries shows that injury to the public credit, injury to confidence in contracts, injury to confidence in investments, brings its misfortune first upon the poor classes, and particularly upon tHe labouring men. We have had many discussions in this House as to
the benefit conferred upon the country by large sums of money being brought in here for investment. I fancy there is no man who has given careful consideration to the affairs of Canada who will not agree, that there is perhaps no country in the world which is in a position to profit so largely as Canada would, by the investment of capital from other countries where it has accumulated and where it cannot be as profitably used as it can be here. I can conceive of no more fatal blow that we could strike at that confidence, which we are happy to say has always been displayed in regard to Canadian securities, than that we should deliberately assume the power to alter to even the extent of one letter a contract that has been deliberately entered into by the parliament of Canada. As has been well said, the Liberal party has no reason to be apologists for this contract in any sense whatever. But, Sir, the Liberal party called upon to administer the affairs of this country must administer them with absolute honour and good faith, so far as the public contracts are concerned.
Hear, hear.

I have had occasion to experience some difficulties in connection with this question. I have addressed public audiences when it would have been more popular for me to use such language as was used by the hon. member for East York, even though I did not wish to be responsible for the meaning of the words I used, as he did not wish to be responsible. I have been called upon to address many audiences where it would have been more popular for me to assume the attitude taken by the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Richardson) and endeavour to confuse the minds of the people, so as to lead them in some way, directly or indirectly, to suppose that there was a way in which this contract could be got around which would relieve them from its effect. I am here to say. that never upon any occasion have I ever taken any other stand than that which I take to-night upon this question. I have expressed the opinion, and I express the opinion now, that I hope and trust there will never be a government in Canada that will be prepared to take the responsibility of introducing legislation to vary or change contracts -which have been fairly and honestly entered into by the parliament of this country. So far as my view of the matter is concerned, it is entirely a question of law. I have been asked a number of times as to what position the government would take in regard to this matter, and I have always said, that so far as 1 was concerned, my view was that the interpretation of the contract must be made by a judicial tribunal, and I further said, that so soon as the twenty years had expired from the date of the ratification of the contract, then, so soon as any municipality was

in a position to bring about a state of circumstances that would give rise to a test case, we would be quite prepared to have that test case carried to court at the expense of the government. I have no doubt that my right hon. friend the Prime Minister is quite in accord with that view, and I believe that nine-tenths of the members of the House will also be in accord with it.
The hon. gnetleman (Hon. Mr. Sifton) has charged me with not stating my views intelligently. I think I did make myself intelligent, and I received an approving nod from the leader of the House.
I protest.

I received an approving nod from the leader of the House when i said that he claimed as one of the great credits to his party, that he had negotiated with the Canadian Pacific Railway for the abandonment of some of their monopolies and the reduction of their rates. These gentlemen opposite have gone up and down the country making stump speeches to the same effect.
Order.
What V
Spoken.

There is an amendment moved, and I have a perfect right to speak to the amendment. One reason why this Bill should not be hoisted for six months is. that parliament can maintain the sanctity of contracts and still right the wrongs of the settlers of the North-west. That is what this parliament can do, and that is what 1 advocate here to-night. It may be by compensation, and even if it has to be by compensation let it be done. Whatever way it be done, the Liberal party, in doing it, will only be vindicating the policy they announced twenty years ago, when they denounced this contract as an injustice to the settler. Even at this late date it is incumbent on the Liberal party to rectify that wrong. My argument was wholly on the line of the Crow's Nest Pass deal, namely, that when the Canadian Pacific Railway next comes to the government they can say to them : We will entertain the proposition you are making, but we want you to surrender that monopoly clause, which is a grievance to the people of the North-west Territories. That is what I argued, and if that is socialism, I am sorry to hear that the Minister of the Interior is not a believer in that kind of socialism, and that he tells the public of Canada and the settlers in the North-west that there is nothing else for the members of this House to do than to maintain the

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: syndicate contract. They have more than that to do. Their duty is to rectify the wrongs of the settlers. These wrongs can be rectified, and the duty and responsibility of rectifying them is upon hon. gentlemen opposite.

Mr. Speaker, I am sorry to see that the House has apparently taken the position-judging from what most of the speakers have said- that it does not intend to interfere in this matter. 1 am afraid that a good deal of the indifference of members of the House is due to the feeling that it is not their ox that is gored. As long as it is only a Northwest matter, and does not affect the rest of Canada, it is a question for the courts. But if it were a matter which concerned Eastern Canada, and concerned it very deeply, I think ways and means would be found for seeing that if we went to the courts, the play would not be with loaded dice at any rate. We are willing to go to the courts, but we want the law straight to go to the courts on.
Let me give the House a few figures to show what the present condition of affairs means to the North-west. There is at the present time a law of the North-west assembly taxing every quarter section of land under ownership within a statute labour district at the rate of $2.50. Under the law l'or tile organization of school districts, lands owned by homesteaders are taxed at an average rate of $3.50 per quarter section. There are thirty-six sections in a township, sixteen of these belonging to the Canadian Pacific Railway. The company's exemption from taxation in each statute labour township amounts to $1(50, and there are in the North-west I think not less than 300 statute labour districts; so that the total exemption of the company from taxation in statute labour districts amounts to nearly $50,000 a year. There are about 500 school districts in the Territories. The country school districts are allowed to be five miles square. That would give at least twelve sections of Canadian Pacific Railway land in each school district. The average taxation is about $3.50 per quarter section. Taking for the purposes of calculation 300 as tlie number of school districts in the Territories, and not 500, we find that the company's exemptions from taxation in school districts amount to about another $50,000 a year. The point I want to make is this, that there is a tax of $6 on every quarter section of land owned by a settler or homesteader, and we claim that the adjoining section owned by the Canadian Pacific Railway Company should pay an equal amount. What I want to impress on this House is that that means something to the people of the east. Ever since the North-west Territories were organized, the support of the schools and the improvement of the roads
have been carried on by means of a subsidy supplied out of the Dominion treasury, and year after year the plea has been made to this government by the government of the Territories that, because of this exemption of the Canadian Pacific Railway lands from taxation the Dominion treasury should supply the deficiency, and it has been supplying the deficiency and will have to continue to supply it as long as the deficiency exists. Do not make the mistake that this eastern country is not interested in the question of the taxation of the Canadian Pacific Railway lands. This eastern country is paying every year out of the general treasury because of that exemption. The people of the North-west are bearing part of the unjust burden, and you are paying the other part; and it is your question as well as ours whether you are going to continue to bear that burden or make the Canadian Pacific Railway Company bear its share.
The House is instructed that it has no right to interpret its own contract, and that if we touch this contract we break the good faith of this country, and do ourselves a great deal of injury. 1 hope we will never want to break an honest contract, but I trust that we will never submit to be buncoed by the misinterpretation of a statute. The right hon. the First Minister said that he agreed with the understanding of the House at the time, as that understanding was explained by the hon. member who moved the Bill, but unfortunately that was not what was embodied in the contract. If that be the case, I say that the understanding of the House at the time was our side of the contract, and it is our business to see that that understanding is maintained, and we are not acting fairly by the people if we do not. This House is not an ordinary party to a contract. When, in the course of debate, questions are addressed to ministers, the positions taken by ministers with regard to those questions, as taken down by ' Hansard,' are accepted as interpreting the law. That should be so, and is so.
It is not so.

Well, I will have to accept the correction, for I certainly am not in a position to give instances to the contrary, but I know of instances in which such statements have been accepted as interpreting the law. I say that the bargain maxle at the time was understood by this country and parliament as having a certain effect, namely, that on the 14th February, now passed, the exemption from taxation terminated, and I say it is the duty of this House to see that the people are not robbed of $50,000 or $100,000 a year through a misinterpretation of the contract.
For my part, I do not admit that there is properly any necessity for the introduction of this Bill. I do not admit that there is any necessity for any interpretation of the contract, or any room for any misinterpretation of it. The necessity for the Bill has arisen from the doubts thrown upon the meaning of the contract by members of the government, as stated in the preamble. I am at the disadvantage of not being learned in the law, and of talcing a position entirely opposite to that taken by some members who are learned in the law, but I say that the words in this Act can have only one meaning, according to my understanding of the English language. The words in dispute, as mentioned by the Solicitor General, are :
Shall also be free from such taxation for twenty years after the grant thereof from the Crown.
I say that the word ' grant ' means ' gift.' That is the dictionary meaning of the word, and it is not right to import into that word the technical legal meaning of ' patent.' I say that the land was given when the Act was assented to, and that the twenty years exemption has to run from that time. Do you tell me that the ownership did not begin until certain acts had been done ? But does not the homesteader, who makes a homestead entry, become in law the proprietor of his land at that moment, 'although he has not completed the homestead duties, and need not complete them for three years afterwards ? And is he not taxable for that land, as soon as he enters it as a homestead. And if he does not pay his taxes until he gets his patent, the land is then sold, and the back taxes are collected out of the proceeds.
There is no such law. The land cannot be sold for the taxes.

When a homesteader enters for his land, that land thereupon becomes assessable, and is assessed. An assessment is placed against that land each succeeding year, and if the taxes are not paid until the patent is secured, then the land can be and is sold for the taxes. Of course it cannot be sold until the patent is secured, but those taxes stand against it until it is patented.

The hon. gentleman is entirely mistaken. The taxes assessed against the land before it is patented cannot be collected from that land. No title can be conveyed in the case of land sold for taxes assessed before the patent is issued.

I have seen hundreds of cases of lands advertised for sale for taxes, and no doubt so has the

lion, the Minister of the Interior, and you will find printed at the end of the list ' unpatented.'
They cannot give a title for these lands.
They may not, but they are sold for taxes.

No one who goes to a sale for taxes and knows anything of the subject will buy any land that is unpatented. Time and again in the courts of Manitoba such sales have been set aside, and the most emphatic declarations made by the courts that lands cannot be sold or titles conveyed in respect of taxes assessed before the patent is issued. The provincial legislature can make the debt a personal one, but cannot convey the lands.

As regards the point whether land that is homesteaded can be taxed before it is patented, I cannot tell you what the law is, as I am not a lawyer. I can only tell you what is done. There is another case. Land is purchased sometimes under an agreement of sale. In such case, who has the ownership of that land, and who is taxed for it up to the time the agreement is completed and the last money paid ?
I say that the ownership of the land for the purposes of this Act commenced when the Act was assented to. As the company could negotiate its business on the strength of the money grant that was given by the Act, just so it could negotiate its business on the strength of the land grants given by the Act. It was given then, and the company proceeded forthwith to do business on it, because it was given. I am astonished to hear the contention that this land grant is not taxable until twenty years after it is patented. I understand that there are members who make that contention. If there are, do they understand the position in which it places them ? Do they understand the position in which it places this country ? Do they know that if that contention is admitted, so far from this exemption having expired at the time this whole country expected it to expire, inasmuch as not an acre of that land has been patented the twenty years exemption has not begun to run; and this country is robbed -I say robbed-for at least twenty years to come of whatever taxes they should have received, but for that exemption. Surely, the Prime Minister is not going to take that position ? Then, is he going to leave it to the chance of a judicial decision on a bunco Act as to whether we shall he robbed for that twenty years or not ? I cannot agree with him, that that is the duty of parliament or of this government. I cannot agree with him that we can afford to stand aside and let ourselves be robbed to any .such tune as that : because, whatever may be the strict legal interpretation of that Act. neither he nor any other man can contend that

it was in the mind of parliament-can contend that it was not furthest away from the mind of parliament at the passing of this Act-that any such contingency should arise. Would any man argue for a moment that, if it had been presented to parliament that that exemption was liable to extend for forty years it would have been granted ? Nobody would contend such a thing.
Oh, yes, they do.
No one.
Yes, 1 have heard it tonight.
Not with the cold facts before them ?
The hon. gentleman (Mr. Maclean) means that the Tories would have given it for fifty years if they had been asked.

I say that if there had been any such idea in the mind of parliament at the time, it would have been brought out in the debate. But there was no such idea brought out in debate, nor was there any such idea in the mind of the country at that time. Those who desire, then, to take the position that this country is liable to the chance of a judicial decision on an Act which they themselves say they do not understand, may say that that is their duty ; but, so far as I am concerned, it is not my duty as a member of this House, as I understand it. I claim that the position of the members of this House Is not the same as that of a private individual. It is the business of this House to see that justice is done to the people of this country ; it is the business of tin's House to see that Acts which are faulty when they are passed are amended and made right, so that there shall be justice and substantial justice to the people of this country. This House is taking too great a responsibility when it says : We will do nothing in the matter ; we will throw it into the courts and let the people take chances on a judicial decision on an Act which we do not pretend to understand, though we know and every man kuows. what was meant when the Act was passed by the parliament who passed it. It has not been shown that there was anything different in the mind of parliament when the Act was passed than I have stated. If it can be shown that parliament had any other idea, that parliament thought exemption would extend for twenty-five or thirty or forty or fifty years, it was competent for any hon. member to show that. But it cannot be shown. There is no doubt that the country and parliament, on behalf of the country, made that bargain with the full belief that the exemption from taxation would terminate on the 15th February, 1901. Then,, if the understanding of parliament is not distinctly and clearly provided for in the Act,

it is the duty, as it is the right-and as it is admitted to be the right-of this parliament to make the Act as parliament understood it to be, and thereby protect the interests of the people of the western country and protect the treasury iu which both east and west are interested.

I ventured to express dissent to a remark of my hon. friend from Alberta, and I only rise for the purpose of explaining why 1 did so. Like him, I have not the good fortune or misfortune, that being a matter of opinion, of being a member of the legal profession. But I think that the principle involved in the Bill now before the House is so simple that even a layman could understand it and find reasons for voting against it. I understand my hon. friend to lay down the principle that the intention of parliament respecting an Act is to be learned from the discussions which took place in parliament. To that I said ' no.' Now, I venture to say that it is not necessary that one should be a member of the legal profession to reach the conclusion that the meaning of an Act of parliament must be gathered from within the four corners of the Act itself. As to coming to the reports of the debates of parliament and finding out what A, B, or C said he meant by that Act, I think no court would entertain that idea. I can give one or two notable instances in which that point had to be considered. One case, if I mistake not, arose in connection with this very contract. I remember, though I need hardly say I was not a member of this parliament at that time, that the question came up as to the meaning of the clause which has been referred to by the hon. member for East York (Mr. Macilean), providing that within a certain period no lines of railway should be constructed south of the Canadian Pacific Railway. When the matter was before parliament, the question was asked what that meant. I think I am correct in saying that a very prominent man who occupied an independent position in this House, Hon. Wm. McDougall, said he attached great importance to that and wanted an explanation of it. Then Sir John Macdonald, replying, said that that clause could only affect the Northwest Territories, which were subject to the government and under the control of this parliament, but could not affect the organized province of Manitoba ; and he used the very famous expression, 'You cannot check Manitoba.' Yet, when, a few years afterwards, the province of Manitoba, under that interpretation, tried to exercise the right to charter lines running to the United States, we were told, notwithstanding the assurance of Sir John Macdonald, that that was not the meaning of the contract, and it must be interpreted as it was, and not as Sir John Macdonald or anybody else said it should be.
speakername: The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Hon. W. S. Fielding).

speechtext: Might I interrupt to suggest a correction, and that is that the action of the government of Sir John Macdonald in disallowing the Manitoba railway charters was not come to on a point of law, but was a matter of policy.
And I believe that the government of Sir John Macdonald determined that they could not allow the claim of Manitoba until they had obtained the consent of the Canadian Pacific Railway.
That is the way out of it.

That confirms my statement that not what Sir John Macdonald said but what the Act of parliament said must be the law of the land. I can give the hon. gentleman another illustration in a matter with which he is not familiar, because it arose in the history of my own province. It arose at a time when the office of Attorney General was occupied by an able lawyer, who afterwards became Prime Minister of this Dominion, the late lamented Sir John Thompson. The contract was made with a railway company, that is the class of contract in which these troubles arise chiefly. A question arose as to the meaning of a certain clause. Sir John Thompson gave his opinion, offhand, that it meant a certain thing. The House accepted that, and the country accepted it. Not many weeks afterwards. Sir John Thompson, in his capacity as Attorney General, was called upon to interpret that contract, and he interpreted it to mean, not what he had said it was. but what, in his judgment as a lawyer, the written Act of parliament meant. But nobody ever assumed that because Sir John Thompson said in parliament it meant something else, therefore it must be held to mean something else. Now, I think that is so simple a matter that even I, as a layman, may properly come to a conclusion at once. We are not called upon to discuss whether the Canadian Pacific Railway contract is a good or a bad contract; we are not called upon even to discuss, however much we may sympathise with the hon. member for Alberta as to the grievance of the North-west, we are not called upon to consider that tonight.
Does not the hon. minister sympathize with the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Richardson) also ?

Well, the hon. member for Lisgar was said by somebody to-night to be a socialist; and my right hon. friend said something about socialism which gave offence to the distinguished socialist from East York (Mr. Maclean), who said he was a socialist of a cer-I tain kind. The right hon. premier did not



object to socialism of a good kind. There may be a wholesome socialism ; but the kind of socialism the Prime Minister objected to was the socialism of this Bill, which proposes that we, one of the parties to a contract, should interpret it in our own interest against the other party. That is a kind of socialism which this parliament has never adopted.
It is not socialism.

My hon. friend from Cape Breton, who, I believe, represents a good kind of socialism, dissents at once from that. Now, I want to say again that we are not called upon to consider to-night whether this was a good or a bad contract, or what Mr. Blake said, or what anybody else said ; and we are not called upon to consider whether the Northwest has a grievance to-day in this matter. Tlie only thing that we are called upon to consider is whether this is a matter for parliament, or whether this is a matter for the courts of the country, to deal with. I think tlie hon. member for Alberta made a pretty good argument to show what this means. I think if I were chief justice of the Supreme Court of Canada I might be disposed to agree with him ; but we are none of us here exercising the functions of the Supreme Court. If there is one thing more than another which we all recognize, it is that the interpretation of contracts shall be determined by the courts and not by parliament. That would be true, even if we had no contract interest ourselves. But when we have, the very fact that we are ourselves a party to a contract, and that we propose to interpret it against the other party-surely. I think the hon. member for Lisgar will not press that matter any further. I agree with all that was said by my colleague, the Minister of the Interior, as to the sacredness of these contracts. Let the idea once get abroad that the parliament of Canada is goiug to undertake to interpret its contracts for itself rather than submit them to the judicial tribunals of the country, and I venture to say from that time forward there would not be the slightest faith in anything this parliament might do upon which a dollar might be required for any public purpose in Canada.

I think the hon. gentleman has furnished, in his brief speech, the strongest possible reason why this Bill should be passed. He has laid down the proposition that tlie courts shall take no cognizance whatever of a debate that may have occurred, or of the understanding that prevailed when a contract was made. Now. this is not a verbal understanding, let me remind the Minister of Finance. There were not certain words passed verbally between members of both sides of tlie House and the syndicate ; but the understanding was taken down in black and white

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: by ' Hansard,' and remains in ' Hansard ' up to the present time. I do not think even the hon. gentleman himself will contend that there is not some doubt at least in that clause itself. He will not contend that it is absolutely sure that the twenty years does not run from the date of the contract. I think the Solicitor General was willing to go that far, and he is the only one, so far as I know, who ever made that admission.
What admission ?
That the language cannot be interpreted to mean that the twenty years began -with tlie ratification of the contract.
Undoubtedly.

I claim that you can read into that clause easily, auy layman, at least, can read into that clause, what it did mean ; and certainly the many able members on both sides of tlie House who spoke when that contract went through, understood what it meant, is the Solicitor General, or is any legal man to-day, able to say that they did not so understand it, or can he say that his opinion or tlie opinion of any other man at present, is better than the opinion of the members who sat on both sides of the House when that contract went through, and who clearly declared-because I quoted their utterances- that they understood that the twenty years would date from the ratification of that contract ?
If, therefore, the proposition of the Minister of Finance is correct, that the courts must take no cognizance wnatever of the understanding, not a verbal understanding, but a distinct printed understanding at that time, then why should we not pass an Act to-night and declare what parliament did intend ? I do not propose, so far as I am concerned, as a representative of the Northwest, to take any risk in the matter ; I do not propose to agree to a reference of this point to the courts. I claim, with the hon. member for Alberta, that it is perfectly clear what parliament intended. Parliament is supreme, far above any superior court, or even any judicial committee of the Privy Council, and let parliament say to-night what was intended. Let parliament protect the vested interests of the people. Why, we hear about ' the monstrous proposition of interfering with vested interests of these stockholders.' Let me tell you, Sir. Speaker, that when these bonds were sold, the men who bought them had the right to investigate that contract, and if they were honest men, if they were shrewd men, they had the very clauses of that contract before them, and having bought their bonds after reading the clauses of the contract, then, on their own heads let the consequences rest. The duty of this House is not to pro-

tect the bondholders of Holland and other countries, but the interests of the people, and it is for their interest that we stand up to-night.
I am not afraid of being called a socialist to-night, I am .proud to be a socialist, if socialism is standing up for the interests of the people. I do not think, from what we see here, that many people understand what socialism is. What is socialism ? It is serving the interests of the people as against private or corporate interests ; it is taking hold of public franchises and running them in the interests of the people. Is that a crime ? Is it anything for which any man need be ashamed ? I do not think it is.
